CHICAGO, July 2l.-A special dispatch from
Goshen, Ind. says: There is hardly doubt
now that the Toledo and Chicago Bee line, the
new short line from Toledo to Chicago, will be
completed before snow flies. The right of way
from Toledo to Goshen is purchased and the
contracts for building the road the greater
part of this distance have already been let.
The projectors are the people Of the Brice-
Thomas syndicate. The road will furnish
a short entrance to Chicago for the Wabash.
the Lake Erie and Western, the Monon and the
Canadian Pacific. The Wabash people will
furnish the greater part Of the money necessary
to complete the line to LapOrte, Ind, and from
there the Lake Erie and Western will furnish
means for construction of the line to Chicago.
The shops will be located here, this being the
halfway point and the citizens having offered
land and over sc, 900 cash for them.

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 22--The fight tonight at
the Olympic Club between Tommy Warren and
Cal Mccarthy was a grand success. II was ap-
pretended that on account of the grand Jury
Indictment against the principals the match
would not come of, but the state law allows
contests with fye-ounce gloves in regu-
larry chartered organizations. Hence
when Acting Mayor Clark received the
opinion OF City Attorney Hunt that the city Of
hcials could not refuse permission to the club
there was general rejoicing by the sporting
fraternity. Mccarthy and Warren were in
structed BY the referee that decision would be
made when il became apparent that one or the
others chances to win had passed. The
men weighed in under the 1lS-pound
limit. The purse was $50, of which
sl,2OO goes to the winner and $500 TO the loser
John Duffy was referee. Haley and Robinson
seconded Warren, and O'Mara and Brown
seconded Mccarthy. Il was one of the prettiest
and gamiest featherweight battles ever seen in
the South, Mccarthy winning in the twenty
first round


In the first round both men displayed great
cleverness from the start. Mccarthy had the
longer reach and showed up stronger, ana both
these qualities told all through the fight. War
rem displayed his usual skill in ducking, but
Mccarthy found a way to stop the
lodging by terrific upper cutting
with his left Notwithstanding this Warren
H.
curing clinches he ran counter to McCarthy's
right, which opened gap over his eye. Thus
the fight stood up to the tenth round
ana from that time out Mccarthy was
general enough TO keep playing upon the
wounded parts. This was easy, as Warren did
most of the rushing. and McCarthys longer
reach enabled him 10 counter on vulnerable
parts. Between the tenth and twentieth rounds
Warren rallied great deal. He stopped num-
Der of vicious uppereuts with his elbow,
found his way to McCarthy's heart and stomach
with his left, and swung his right on his neck.
Loss OF blood, however, made him weak, and
his blows scarcely moved Mccarthy, who Kept
Warren's wounds open, and landed often
enough to sting the little Californian to madness
and keep him growing weaker all the time


McCarthys constant battering had the desired
effect Warren lost science as he lost strength,
and, rushing madly, struck aiInessly and wore
himself out He went down frequently in the
twentieth round, and was nearly knocked out
when the gong sounded the close of that round


When he came up for the twenty first round
the fight was plainly hopeless. Mccarthy
countered with his right as he rushed in, and
Warren went down on all fours. He tried hard
TO struggle up before the eight seconds were
called but fell forward on his hands and was
counted out. Mccarthy was without scratch


George Dixon whipped Cal Mccarthy easily.
Dixon fights at lI6 pounds and calls himself the
bantam champion OF the world.l

PITTsBURa, March 21.--A desperate
shooting affray occurred in house at
Peters Run, near McKeesport, tonight,
resulting in the killing Of one detective,
the serious wounding of another and
the slight wounding OF tive policemen
and woman. Six weeks ago girl
named Laura Hill entered the jewelry
store at Homestead and began pricing
jewelry. While the proprietor was thus
engaged three men forced an entrance
from the rear, struck the proprie-
tor down, cleaned out the store
and escaped with $500 in
cash and jewelry. The Wilkinson
detective agency was given charge Of
the case, and not long after the girl was
arrested in Harrisburg. She confessed,
and acting on her instructions tonight,
Chief Detective Wilkinson, with De-
tective Murphy and two McKeesport
policemen, went to the house Of the
leader in the robbery, A. G. Budd, at
Peters Run. The girl must have warn
ed Budd, for when Wilkinson threw
open the door, Budd threw up revolver
and fred, killing Wilkinson. Detective
Murphy leaped over his prostrate form,
and facing Budd, a terrible duel at short
range followed. Budd emptied one re-
volver, and his wife, who was in the room,
ran to his assistance with another.
Murphy, though badly wounded, had
also emptied his pistol, and STOPPING to
the dead body OF his chief, drew his re-
volver and renewed firing. He was
firing blindly into the smoke, however,
while the burglar centered all his shots
toward the door. Suddenly the woman
screamed, and Immediately after MUIR
ply fell with bullet in his
breast. During the panic that
seized the two policemen at this
second loss to their ranks, Budd es-
capped. A review Of the room showed
Wilkinson dead, Murphy shot in the
face and breast, while the woman re-
ceived shot in the arm, and the two
policemen were slightly wounded by
flying bullets. The woman was taken to
jail, while kilograms were sent all over
to intercept Budd. He is noted crook.

county has again been visited by dis
astrous rain and wind storm, con tinu-
ing until O'Clock this morning. Rail
road creek reached height only two
feet lower than high water mark last
month, when it wrought such terrible
havoc. Many residents of the flats be-
came frightened and deserted their
homes. Two houses which were re-
moved from their foundations by the
former flood were this morning carried
into the Sioux river and dashed to pieces
against the Second street bridge. The
timbers and ruins of the last flood we're
also swept against the bridge, which
went out early this morning. Two other
bridges in the city were also carried
away. There are washouts on the
Illinois Central between here and Sioux
City, also on the Cherokee division north
and south of here. Crops are greatly
damaged.

New YORK, April 20.-A terrible
tragedy was enacted in the Italian
quarter of Hoboken early this morning.
Angelo Gaboth and wife came to spend
the night at the home OF Mrs. Gaboth's
parents, Antonio Chinchilla and wife.
Gaboth was a shiftless fellow, and in
view of the tragedy, it is probable last
nights visit was deliberate plot to rob
the Chinchillas. About one O'Clock this
morning Gaboth arose, and entering the
room where his wife was sleeping
with her mother, plunged a sti-
letto into the old woman's abdomen,
killing her. The fact that his wife re-
manned perfectly quiet, with her
mothers blood squirting over her, is
taken as evidence that she was party
to the horrible plot. Gaboth then went
into the next room, and thrust his
stiletto into the neck of old Chinchilla,
meaning to end his father-in-law' life
with one blow. He missed the vital
spot, however, ,and the old man gave cry,
which aroused his two sons in the next
room. One of them seized stiletto and
sprang at the murderer like tiger. A
fierce contest followed, the men fighting
up and down the room, and striking at
each other. Suddenly Gaboth's wife
sprang out of bed and tried to separate
the combauants, receiving two serious
stabs. The older of the sons seized her,
pulled her away, and let the combatants
fight it out. A moment later Gaboth
flung up his arms with loud cry and
fell dead. Young Chinchilla had driven
a stiletto through his left eye into his
brain. Young Chinchilla went at once
to the police station and reported the
occurrence. He was seriously cut. His
sisters injuries are not dangerous, but
the old man will probably die. The
bodies Of Mrs. Chinchilla and Gaboth

when the body arrived from Washing
ton, it had lain in state at Grace church,
where it was viewed by hundreds OF
citizens. The services were conducted
by the Rev. w. G.. Foute, of Grace
church, and the building was crowded

Mayor Sanderson, Chief Justice Beatty
and other prominent men of the state.

all day, thousands of people who could
not gain admittance to the church lined
the streets to view the funeral process
sion. In the funeral procession were
the second brigade, N.G.C., the con-
gressional committee, legislative COM

Democratic state central committee of
California, state Democratic club,
Iroquois club and many civic organiza-
tions.


Grace church was elaborately Gecorat-
ed with evergreens and flowers, and
numerous floral pieces were sent by
friends. The closing ceremonies at the
cemetery were very simple. Six soldiers
lifted the casket and bore it between
files of the pall-bearers to raised plat
form, which surrounded the vault. Rev.
Or. Foute took up the closing portion of
the Episcopal burial service, and the
final words of peace were uttered.

prisoners.


With the exception of little scorching

There was a side-splitting scene in
Justice Stanton's court yesterday after
noon. Mrs. Anna Crosse, a woman who
runs bakery at the corner OF Rose and
First street, was on trial for threatening
to kill Mrs. Eva Dickhof, a neighbor.
The defendant was Dutch, the prose-
cutting witness was of the same nation
ality and the attorneys for the defense
came from Germany. The court room
smelled of beer and Limberger during
the trial and the testimony was Of pc
culiarly Teutonic character. Mrs.
Crosse and Mrs. Dickhoff have been
enemies long time. They began by
calling each other "mean old things"
or words to that effect and their strained
relations finally parted entirely and
actual war was the result.


The melting cause of the final grand
rumpus between the females was the re-
ceipt by Mrs. Crosse of two comic val
entines, which had been scrlbbled over
with verses in German and English.
Whoever wrote those verses was "hate-
full creature" so Mrs. Crosse thought,
and she was probably right. The fol-
lowing Is sample:


MADAM


You are a darling:


Your husband is dear,
oh If you only knew how often


He and l together drink our beerl


You think you are darling;
You think it's very nice
To own baker shop
And keep your beer on ice.


The day is not far distant
When you will come to grief,
And the time between your death
And our marriage Will be brief.


And then, my darling baker woman,
We will often pray for thee,


And after we are married


We will call the child o. D.
Your friend, KATHERINE.


Some of the other writings on the val
entines were hardly printable, and the
pictures themselves, though rather in
appropriate, were probably vile enough
to suit the purposes of the sender. Miss
Schenck, pretty little German girl,
was put on the stand and testified be-
tween spasms of weeping that she wrote
the German on the valentines at the re-
quest of Mrs. Dickhof. Mrs. Dickhoff
had received the valentines through the
mail, and she was sure Mrs. Crosse sent
them to her. So she got the witness to
add some more to the writing that was
already on them and sent them back.
The witness sobbed bitterly when she
was asked to translate the German. 1t
was ''too nasty" she said, and the floor
was slippery about the witness box when
she took her seat.


When Mrs. Crosse got the valentine
with the verses about her husband
drinking beer with Mrs. Dickhoff she
was very wroth. In fact words could
not express her feelings at that time.
She had no doubt that Mrs. Dickhoff
wrote them, SO she took an iron bar and
pounded on the door of her neighbor.
Mrs. Dickhoff came to the door, and the
fur few for time, until the women
were separated, when the darling
baker woman" left the house, vowing
to kill Mrs. Dickheff. The latter's hus-
band therefore swore out warrant for
the arrest of Mrs. Crosse on charge of
threatening to kill his wife. Justice
Stanton, after hearing the testimony,
held the defendant in 500 bonds to
keep the peace.

F. G. Jefferson, of Toronto, Canada,

"The following case has come under my
notice: A farmer married his cousin, and
both possessed all their faculties, and
they have nine children, of whom five
daughters were born deaf mutes. Three
of these daughters married speaking and
hearing husbands. The first one has
three deaf mute children out of five, the
second one has two deaf mute children
out of three and the third has one deaf
mute child out Of two. This proves that
Professor Bell, Of Washington, United
States, has made mistake by publish
ing largely that the intermarriages of
deaf mutes bring a deaf mute race, when
the fact is that deaf mute children pro-
ceed from married cousins possessing all
their faculties. In the Belleville deaf
mute school there are 240 pupils, and not
one of them has deaf mute parents.
There are many other similar cases in
England and the States"

ricane force, and the seas ran mountain

geoD. half bitched up, over nineteen years.

ence with her lover and consented to elGpe.

New ORLEANS, Sept. 17.-There is
considerable excitement over the grand
jury's reported interference with the
Mccarthy Warren fight before the
Olympic club next Tuesday night. The
state law permits glove contests before
regularly chartered athletic clubs. The
present grand jury, which has only
been in existence two weeks, is
very moral body and started in
on prize fights without much delay.
Owing to the law their future course is
hardly apparent. They examined the
chief OF police and several police cap
tains and the officers of the Olympic
club. The jury held long session, re-
viewing their statements and examin-
ing the law. The outlook is that the
grand jury will make its report tomor-
row and will call upon the proper
authorities to stop the Mccarthy War
rem fight.

NORFOLK Va.), March 27.-The Nor
wegGn bark Dictator, from Pensacola, Fla,
for England, with lumber and carrying a
crew Of fifteen and the captains young wife
and three-year-old boy, came ashore in a
strong easterly gale this morning two miles
north of the Virginia Beach Hotel The
weather was so thick that the vessel was
not seenIuntil O'Clock, and then she was in
the breakers quarter of a mile from shore.
The crews from the two life-saying stations
were promptly on hand, but could not use
the boats because of the tremendous surf.
They tried repeatedly to fire the life line
over the ship, but the guns could not deliver
the lines so far.


The ship finally succeeded In getting a
line ashore, tied TO barrel, which the surf
carried in. A breeches-buoy was quickly
rigged and sent out, but unfortunately the
sailors seemed ignorant of its use, and the
work was delayed until the life-savers wrote
instructions and sent them to the ship in a
bottle over the lifeline. The crew then pro-
ceeded to carry out the directions. The first
man was delivered ashore in eight minutes,

and seven others were rescued before sun
set, four coming in a life-boat, which was
capsized in the surf. They were rescued
with great difficulty In half-dead condi-
tion. The beach WAS lined with people from
country houses and the hotel, and to the
spectators the anxiety and suspense was
awful


AT nightfall there were still nine persons
on board. including the captain, his wife
and little child. The captain urged his wife
all day to take the buoy ami 90 ashore, but
she steadfastly refused to leave her husband
and child, as only one could be brought at a
time.


Soon after dark the bark went to pieces
in tremendous sea, and the captains wife
and six sailors were lost. just before the
ship broke up the captain jumped into the
sea with his son strapped to his back and
reached the shore alive, but the boy was
lost, making a total of eight lives.


The list of the saved is: Captain J, H.
Jorgenson, Second Mate Anderson and
seven sailors. The captain reports he was
trying to make Hampton Roads, having
been disabled by a hurricane since the 10Th
inst. For four DAYS the sun had not been
seen and the weather was so thick last night
that they struck the breakers before they
could see the coast.

BAN LUIS OBIsPo, April 20.-The corpse
of a man named Charles French was dis
covered Saturday afternoon under circum-
stances showing a slow, lingering death
from starvation, shock and exposure.
French was living alone upon his claim,
about three miles east of Pozo, in this
county, and was missed from his cabin
about eight days before the discovery OF his
body. Search was made without success,
but finally the neighbors found the body of
the poor wretch pinned to the earth by a
tree which he had felled, and which had
fallen across his thighs, preventing
any movement. His cries could not
be heard and he had evidently worked and
struggled desperately but vainly to release
himself with his knife. He had dug away
at the hard earth and his torn and bloody
finger-nails showed the terrible efforts he
had made. He had to lie there through the
cold and stormy nights and the long days
until death released him. When found de-
composition had set in, and in the attempt
to remove the body the flesh stripped from
the bones. The verdict of the Coroner'S
Jury was in accordance with these facts.

Once Nebraska had been to visit at their

was nearly dark but as it was a moonlight
night she did not feel lonely, and had just
thought, What lovely evening for a
rideY' when she heard patteriDg steps.
Looking around, she saw two wolves
stealthily following. She urged her pony
to his greatest speed, and tried to think out
what she should do, for she was by this
time only hallway home. and seven miles
from the nearest house.


She kept perfectly still because she knew
that if she screamed before she was at
tackled. although it would scare the animals
away for time, they would return, and
would soon get used to the noise and not be
frightened by it. She felt certain so few of
them would net dare attack her, for wolves
are very cowardly. but she also knew that
they would summon the rest of the pack
almost instantly.


The wolves were now in full pursuit, and
she, glancing back, saw there were three
She was alarmed indeed now, and as they
were gaining on her every minute, she knew
something must be done if she was to reach
home alive. She knew the wolves would
not long hesitate to attack her, for there
was quite large pack of them gathering.
Her pony, too, shifted danger, and the next
instant, before she cOmprehended what he
was going to do, he had turned and sprung
right into the midst of the snarling pack,
paving and kicking right and left.


He mad not forgotten his wild habits, nor
how he had many times saved himself from
the ferOcious animals. And now his
bravery stood his mistress in good stead.
for as his feet came down on the wolves
fierce yelps showed that he was not dealing
gentle taps. In few seconds there were
four stretched dead on the ground, and the
others had fed.


The young rider had thought, as soon as
she knew what lie was going to do, that she
was safe If she could keep on his back, and
this required all her strength and skill.
When the pack was gone she looked down
at the dead bodies, and shuddered as she
thought of her narrow escape. With no
injuries and only a few anxious minutes.
she had secured four dead wolves, worth
more than $50.


She dismounted and slung them over Paw
nee's back and then gaIloped home.


No need of saying that her father and
mother Were surprised to see her come up
to the door and exhibit triumphantly four
slain wolvesl


After his glorious exploit the pony was
more cited than before. Did he not de-
serve it?-Kate Nj. Putney in st. Nicholas

CHICAGO, August 25.-The workmen
in the new four-mile tunnel under Lake
Michigan, for increased water facilities
for the city, struck pocket of gas
today. The pressure of the air
in the tunnel was raised to twenty
four pounds to the square inch,
keeping back the gas, but tonight this
became too oppressive for the workmen,
and it was lowered to sixteen pounds.
Late tonight the electric lights at a
point two miles and half from shore
got out of order, and man went out to
repair them. When he went near the
point where the gas was escaping, it
ignited from his torch. and tremendous
explosion followed. One man was fatally
and seven others seriously injured.

Many mine shows vein of metal when

One of the myriad little children who live

tered vehicle was her kitten, a sorry-looking
thing, but the only pet she had. She came

then he launched himself into the group of
heartless rowdies. He was match for them
at their best, and In moment they had scat
tered and fled. The little girl had been
penned in doorway and could not escape.
He saw her, the tears cutting pitiful white
down her dirty. frightened face, and he
stopped and gathered her in his arms.


Come, Oh, my beauty" he said, with
heartiness. We'll buy another barrow"
And he carried her into the nearest store
where everything is kept and anything is
sold and found the thing she wanted. The
dealer had seen-as had the entire block
the kick. the punishment and the generous
effort to tighten the chid's heart, and he set
a handsome price on the whcelbarrow But
the roupder paid it-paid it royally-and
walked home behind the little girl and her
kitten as proud as king.


There probably wasn't nobler thing done

ist programme, the British declaring

ful legislation. We must forcibly ex-

listing conditions." After resolution

Semitism as a device of capitalists to
SOW mischief among workingmen, while
many speakers reminded the congress

also great oppressors. Finally resolu-
ton was passed cohdemning both anti
Semitism and Jewish financial tyranny.
This impossibility of reconciling con-
Aicting opinions and interests is the
key note Of the whole proceedings of the
congress, its discussions leading to no
practical result.

HALIFAX, N. s., July 19.--Particulars
were received by mail today of har-
rowing disaster on the Newfoundland
coast, the schooner Publico Belle being
wrecked and two women and five chill
dren lost. Captain Samuel Butts, of the
lost vessel, states that the Publico Belle
with crew of four men left Catalina on
the morning of Wednesday, the .Sth
inst, bound for st. Johns, with cargo
of lumber. She had also on board five
women and five children as passengers.
There came on storm Of wind and
rain, lasting from IL 80 Wednesday
night until daylight Thursday morn
ing. The vessel lost her mainsail
and foresail, successfully, and ran
ashore on cliff at 2:3O O'Clock
Thursday morning. The crew let go an
anchor, which checked the vessel, but
the chain parted. William Rose jumped
ashore and the captain threw line to
him. By this means the rest of the
crew got ashore. The following passen-
gers were saved: Mrs. Rachel Burton,
Miss Julia Burton and Miss Wells. Mrs.
Freeman and Miss Caroline Higgins
were drowned, and three children were
also lost.


Miss Wells writes: II was sitting on
the locker and Miss Higgins was lying
on part OF it; all the others, the chill
dren included, were in their berths.
One of the crew came down for rope.
We asked him if there was 4 chance to
be saved. He said: Yes; don't say
anything; it will be all right The water
was then coming through the cabin floor,
and was soon up to the lockers. All the
children were taken out of their berths
and got ready to start for the deck. We
were close into land, but heavy sea
was breaking over the rocks when we
reached the deck. Two of the crew
were ashore, having taken off their
boots and jumped onto the rocks. An
old man had tied rope around his
waist, the other end being held by a
sailor on the rocks. He jumped and
got ashore. The captain was the only
man then left on board. We all went
over to the side where he was. He tied
rope around Miss Burton and she
landed safely. While in the act of plac-
ing rope around Mrs. Burton heavy
sea came and washed all off the deck.
1 caught the end of rope which was
in the captains hand, and was hauled
ashore with him, while wave washed
Mrs. Burton upon the rock, but never
saw Mrs. Freeman or Miss Higgins
again. Mrs. Freeman would in all
probability have been saved, had she
abandoned her child, but the mothers
love was too strong"


Miss Wells also told a story Of severe
privations met with before the party
finally came across some men, one of
whom took them to his house and cared
for them. She adds that it is her belief
that all could have been saved had they
been warned sooner.

The British ship Kinkora was lowed into
port last night in distress. She is bound
from Sydney to Portland with cargo Of
COAL


Nothing Of moment occurred until the 26th
OF October. when she was caught in a hurri-
cane that lasted five days. and when it sub
sided left the fine ship almost wreck. The
sea raised by the gale was terrific. swept the
ship from stem to stern and caused her to
labor badly.


Several sails were blown away, but the
final crash came about midnight on the 26th,
when without warning the main-topmast
was carried away at the sleaye-hole. and in
an instant down came the masthead with
the Observation-Disclosures yards and all the
rigging.


The fore-topgallant yard broke in the
sings and came down with a.terrible crash.
while a yardarm fell end OH and went clean
through the deck, tearing hole five feet
square, and did not stop until it landed on
pile of coal in the lower hold.


REFUGE SOUGHT IN THE CABIN.


The mlzZen royal mast also went, taking
the yard with it and nearly all the upper
stays and also the brace pennants were
carried away. The crew sought refuge in
the cabin when the crash came, and by
stroke of good luck no one was injured.


The great amount of spars and gear that
was carried away made the crew think that
everything aloft was coming down by the
run at once. AS soon as the noise caused
by the falling spars ceased the crew began
the dangerous work of clearing away the
wreck, ana it was not until after twenty
four hours Of hard and constant labor that
this was accomplished.


Nearly all the spars were steel, and as the
ship rolled heavily from side TO side the
men had all they could 90 to prevent them
selves from being knocked out of the rigging
or crushed by the wreck Captain Lawrence
was the first into the rigging and worked
like beaver until the last spar was sent
down on the deck.


HEADED FOR THIS PORT.
> The vessel was then made as snug as Dos
sible, and after much-needed rest a sur
vey of the damage was made. In addition
TO the loss of the main-tOpnast and every
thing above II, the mizzen royalmast was
gone, the fore-topmast head sprung and
both fore-topgallant and royal yards carried
away.


Neatly everything aloft was wreck, and
what made matters worse was that, like
most iron ships. the lowermasts and top
maSts are in one, this preventing the crew
making repairs. In this condition Captain
Lawrence decided TO head for this port, and,
considering the damage sustained by the
vessel, she has made good time.


In order TO make the needed repairs the
entire cargo will have to be discharged.
survey will be held and the work Of dis
charging begun.

Between the dawning and the dew,

The following extract from private
letter written from Honolulu by DIR.
George p. Andrews outlines novel
feast:


We have been having festival week,
the semi centennial of Oahu college. A
number of alumni came home from the
states, among others General S. G.. Arm
strong, of Hampton, Va, and he gave
us some grand talks on his work in the
great school there. Rev. William GU
lick and wife also are here from their
twenty years work in Spain. The great
feast was novel sight. An awning of
sails covered in space about 60 by 100
feet, under which were laid tables, and
the viands, cooked la Hawaii, were
laid on them. AS provision was made
for thousand people an account of the
cooking may be of interest.


There were provided forty-fve half
grown pigs, two beeves, 1876 chickens,
several hundred fish, bushels of sweet
potatoes, etc. The larger pigs were cut
into fragments and tied in bundles of
banana and drachma leaves of pound
or two weight each. The beef was
served in the same way, also the chick
ems. The smaller pigs were wrapped
whole in the leaves. Preparations for
the cooking were made the day before.
Four holes were dug, one 10 by feet,
one by feet and the others about
three feet wide and two feet deep. A
quantity of wood was placed in the
grotto and upon this were placed large
stones a foot deep.


One fire was lighted early in the morn
ing of the day before and the second
about o'clock. At 3 o'clock the wood
was burned out and the bottom was
mass of red hot stones Upon these were
spread layer of crushed fresh banana
stems six inches thick, and upon these
were piled the small bundles of meat two
or three feet high and the size of the
hole. Over them was placed mass of
fresh banana leaves several inches thick,
over this mating, and then dirt foot
thick and the imu was finished and left
to steam until the next morning.


At in the evening the big one was
similarly filled with the remainder of the
meat and the trussed pigs, and also cov-
cred. One can imagine what delight
full heat would be brought to bear upon
the contents of the imu, and how deli
cately the contents would be cooked dur
ing the long hours of the night


Early in the morning of the feast day
the two small linus were filled with the
fish tied up in leaves and sweet potatoes
and covered. The large ovens covered
the day before were opened during the
morning and the contents taken out and
covered to keep hot.


The tables seated between 200 and 300
at time. Poi, the native food-a paste
made from the Calocosen esculentum
and soured-was put in small, water
tight baskets along the center of each
table so that four persons could reach
each one with the fingers (knives and
forks are eschewed at "a luan). Each
table was also gay with crimson feshed
watermelons cut in fancy shapes, various
relishes of raw sea urchins, meat, sea-
weed, raw shrimps and pounded kukui
nuts and salt. Conveniently at hand
were fern leaves, and the viands upon
leaves, gourds and wooden bowls and
platters.


The guests recline at their ease on the
left side and eat with the right hand.
Each one has a bowl of fair water to
cleanse the fingers. The method of eat
ing is not disgusting. The natives use
their fingers dexterously and daintily
and not piggishly, though they are
rather gormandizing in their native
state. e.-Detroit Free Press

Margaret Murphy, pretty domestic Of 10
years, is the heroine of South Brooklyn
to-day. She brayely entered the house of

them out, and when they scaled fence she
went over the fence after them, says the
Brooklyn Eagle. When they pointed a re-
volver at her she did not finch, and she
continued the chase for half a mile and
until she saw the two burglars arrested.


Margaret is employed in the family of

will yOu?" asked Margaret. Then
sh0otw and looking into the barrel of the

The burglars ran through lot aud

At Thirty first street Pol ceman Fitzger-

The British steamship Dorian, Capt Donelly,

tain's raft had barely hoated It's own length

From the other raft only three out of the

passed over beam. Kelly's right name

Two Fishermen Rescued After PeriIous


Adventure.


Daniel Keen and Robert Stephenson, net
fishermen at Nerplanck, \. Y, had queer
experience last Sunday afternoon and even
ing, says the Philadelphia Telegraph They
were hauling in their nets on a field of Ice
that seemed safe, but suddenly broke up
and sent them drifting down the river on
one of its pieces. They ran for their lives
when the breaking began, but were too late
TO reach the shore


a thick fog came up and the night was
very dark. A strong ebb tide carried the
cake of ice down the river. The men lighted
their lanterns and Kept up "A continuous
hallooing, but the gale drowned their voices.
1t raIned terribly and there were occasional
flashes Of lightning. The cake Of ice kept
breaking up and the men had to keep jump
ing from piece to piece to save themselves.
Twice Stephenson fell into the water and
was rescued by Keen. The flood tide COM
menced TO make and carried the ice up and
the WIND drove 1t across the river.


The fog lifted for moment and the men
thought they saw light and renewed their
calls, which were heard and answered by a
Waterman of the West Shore Railroad who
quickly summoned help in the persons of
Alexander Ten Eyck, John White and Paul
keesler Of TOmpkins Cove. Ten Eyck got
his boat, and, accompanied by White aud
Keesler, dragged it over the ice until the
water was reached, and then it was quickly
launched. There was a great quantity of
floating ice and very slow progress was made
toward the men, whose cake was fast grow
ing smaller. The water was dashing over
them, and the men lay flat upon the ice to
prevent being washed into the river


The boat finally reached the cake of ice
they were on, but could not get to them
heesler and White broke through into the
water several times, and only saved them
selves by grasping the side of the boat. Keen
and Stephenson crawled toward the boat,
but the ice gave way under them, and they
with difficulty succeeded in getting ia it
again. Finally the painters of the boat were
tied together and thrown to them, and they
were hauled in. As Keen, who was the last
one rescued, was hauled in. the cake of ice
they had been on was dashed into a thou
sand pieces by an immense wave, which
nearly swamped the boat. The men were
taken to Tompkins Cove by their rescuers

weekly crop report was telegraphed to
Washington today: Rain has slightly
damaged hay and ripe fruits in Northern
California, and lodged the heavy growth
of grain in various portions of the state.
Prospects for large yield of wheat and
barley were never better. In Southern
California deciduous fruits are doing
well, except prunes. Apricots will soon

we'll in the Anaheim district. The po-

weather is needed to mature the fruit.


PORTLAND, Ore, June 13.-Dispatches
from points in Eastern Oregon and
Washington state that the heavy rains
of the past few days insure large grain
crop.


The weekly report of the Oregon
weather bureau says that unless very
unusual weather conditions prevail, the
Oregon and Eastern Washington wheat
crop will be the largest ever produced.
The hay crop will be large, and fruit
will be fully an average yield. Hop lice
are becoming more general.

complioe Captured.


TOMBSTONE, Ariz., June 13.-The noted
desperate Geronimo, who had vowed to
kill the late Sheriff j. HI. Slaughter of
this county for his vigorous pursuit and
killing of some of his confederates for
train robbery and murder in Sonora two
years ago, when Express Messenger Hay
was killed, was shot and killed thirty
miles from Benson, Ariz., today. His
two companions were captured, one be-
ing shot in the thigh. There is great
feeling of relief among the inhabitants
over his killing.


The Stars Benson special says: Dep
uty Sheriff Gray arrived here this morn
ing with the body of the notorious Mex
lean stage robber, Geronimo, and two
-confederates. They have been robbing
stages in Southern Arizona during the
last five years. and officers have been
continually after them. Last night
Gray and posse run them down in the
mountains near Pantano. They made
a fight, and Geronimo fired five and
Leon three shots without effect. They
had pistols; their pursuers had rifles.
Geronimo fell dead. Leon surrendered.


Geronimo has robbed the United
States mail aid stage passengers more
than dozen times. He has committed
many murders; was captured several
times and escaped.


Leon, his accomplice, up to six months
ago, was deputy sheriff under Sheriff
Slaughter in almost constant pursuit OF
Geronimo.


This killing and capture is considered
the most important ever made in Ari-
Zona.

LONDON, July 13.-It is reported that
the emperor has invited the prince and
princess of Wales to visit Germany in
full state, the coming autumn, and that
the prince and princess have, with the
consent OF Queen Victoria accepted the
invitation.


The emperor this morning rode
through Hatfield park. Upon his re-
turn to Hatfield house he lunched In
marble hall. All the ambassadors, min
listers and their wives and Mr.. and Mrs.
Joseph Chamberlain were present.


Emperor William returned from Hat
field house this afternoon and proceeded
to Windsor. After an hours conversa-
tion, the queen bade him an affectionate
adieu, and the emperor left for London
where he found the empress and pro-
ceeded with her to the railroad station
where she took train for Felixstowe to
remain with her children.


The emperor dined this evening at the
house of Lady Dudley, with select
number of the aristocratic circle. The
emperor started for Scotland tonight.
As the train left. the station, there was
prolonged cheering by the crowd. In
stead of recognizing the farewell ac-
corded him, with his military style, the
emperor waved his hand.

WASHINGTON, Feb. T.--Under instruc-
tions from the committee ON finance,
Senator Morrill,, chairman of that COM
mittee, today reported adversely Sena-
tor Stanford's bill Ito provide the gov
ernment with means sufficient to sup
ply the national want of sound circu-
lating medium" involving loans on
lands at 2 per cent. interest.


The report contends that land owners,
who will be the only class to be bene-
flied, are too prudent to. cover their
homesteads with mortgages. and even
young men starting in life,
when borrowing capital, do not in
tend to remain years in debt. But the
low rates of interest offered to land own
ers might inspire improvident habits
and extravagant speculation in the
mass of people not free from such temp
tations.


The report says the bill endorses the
principle put forth more than century
ago by the notorious John Law. Expe-
rience has shown that whenever such
reckless experiments, intended to secure
cheap money, have been tried, they
ended in commercial crisis, bank.
ruptcy and national disaster.


The report compares the measure un.
der discussion to the Argentine republic
and colonial schemes, both of which
say the committee, resulted in shame
and disaster.

Intricacy and Significance of Geological


Structure.


Foremost in their geographic Importance,
and in the intricacy and significance Of their
geologic structure and origin, are the noun
tain belts which consist of folded rock for
nations. The strata forming the upper part
of the earth's crust are bent up and down in
long, nearly straight or curvlng, wave-like
ridges and troughs, and where their disturb
ance was greatest and successive ridged
folds are closely pressed together. The
waves Of the rock structure are then pushed
to such steepness that their sides become
parallel with each other, and the entire
fold is driven forward into an inclined
position. The order of the strata on
the lower side of the oppressed fold
Is thus inverted: the originally highest
and last formed deposits. there lie beneath
older beds, in an overturned series Sub
aerial erosion then wears down the undua-
tions and the crests of the closely folded
strata, often planning them off until long
section, crossing mountain ranges, passes
from older TO newer beds and onward from
newer to older. in several alterations, hav-
ing throughout the whole nearly constant
steep dip. Owing to the interbedding of
hard and enduring sandstone, quartZite,
gness and other rock formations, with more
easily erOded limestone, shales, incoherent
sandstones or schlsts, the erosion commonly
produces new topography, making hollows
and long valleys where the more erosible
beds have been removed, and leaving ridges
and mountain ranges of the harder rocks.
More than this. when erosion has been con-
tinue6 through very long periods it tends
toward the ultimate result of removing the
upward curved or anticlinal portions OF the
great folds and sparng the originally lower
downward curved or synclinal portions,
until valleys take the places which were
originally occupied by the highest upheav-
ais, while the original troughs. where the
rocks were most compacted by pressure, re-
main now as the principal mountain ridges.
Under denudation the folded mountainous
belt fulfils the prophecy, Every valley
shall be exalted and every mountain and
hill shall be made low."-POpular Science

palms

Among the graduates of the year one
brave young woman has completed a
course frankly taken in preparation for
matrimony. Like many girls who make
society amusements their chief existence,
this young woman did not realize the
deficiencies in her education until she
had won the friendship and love of one
who was her superior in intellectual ac-
quirements. With the realization Of her
ignorance came the determination to
study for self improvement.


Entering as a pupil at well known
school for girls she took courses in litera-
ture, philosophy and other studies, which
would enable her to write and speak with
accuracy and would teach her the best
methods of thought. She entered classes
of political economy and studied the
newspapers under competent direction.
Urging her teachers to correct all i'm
perfections in her speech and manner,
she made constant effort to attain the
standard which might bring her nearer
to an equality with her future husband.


The struggle was not easy. There
were trials of pride in studying with
girls of a more youthful age; there were
many moments Of modification from
the exposure of her ignorance. Deter
mination to succeed won its usual re-
wards. The society girl, whose bright
mind had been eclipsed by the routine of
pleasures, became renowned in the
school as one of the most earnest and
satisfactory pupils. When she gradu-
ates this year into the refined home that
has been in preparation for her she will
meet her husband upon an equality, and
entertain his friends with feeling of
cheerful confidence


She says that the whole world seems
more stable since she has been sure that
her sentences are grammatical and her
pronunciation according to the best au-
thorities. Boston Journal

SAN DIEGO, July 16.-The interest and
excitement felt throughout the city over
the killing of Brown, seaman OF the
Charleston, and the beating Of his
mates, do not subside, and are not only
shared in by the more excitable ele-
ment, but by responsible, law-respecting
and sober citizens. All last night knots
of men could be seen upon the corners
OF the downtown streets, discussing the
matter, and there was plainly an under
current of determination that justice
shall be done to the offenders. The fact
is generally known that two crowds of
organized men, numbering about fifty,
were banded at two places in the city,
and at the word from any leader would
have joined for an attack upon the Jail.


The testimony introduced before the
coroner's jury today shows that the So
called deputy marshals were entirely to
blame for the trouble, Breedlove, the
leader, having stated the night before
the trouble, that he proposed to take
the sailors next day or some would get
shot. Marshal Gard, on the witness
stand today, testified that Breedlove
and his posse acted entirely without his
authority that Breedlove was not a
deputy United States marshal, nor had
ever been deputized. Breedlove wears a
deputy United States marshal badge
and still claims to be such.


Neither Webb nor Gillespie have yet
been arrested, although warrants are
out for both.


About fifty witnesses have been ex-
amined by the coroner, and theca will
probably go to the jury tomorrow: Feel
ing is SO strong against the prisoners
that they are kept locked in their cells,
instead Of being brought into the court
room. Trouble is feared tonight, and
extra guards have been placed over
them.


Marine burial services were held over
Brown on board the Charleston this
morning, and his remains were then
brought ashore and sent to San Francis-
CO by this afternoon s train.

New YoRK, May 1.--Small armies of
men, marching to the tune of the Mar
sellaise and other airs, carrying red flags
and transparencies, the latter denounc-
ing all monopolies, approached Union
Square tonight from various directions,
to participate in a great eight-hour labor
demonstration, under the auspices of
the Central Labor Federation and the
Socialistic Labor party. Many thous-
and people congregated about various
stands. The main speakers stand was
at Cottage plaza, on Seventeenth street.
Here English speakers talked, while
speeches were delivered in German and
Hebrew from stands on Broadway and
Fourth avenue. Shortly after 8 O'Clock,
the meeting was called to order by Lu-
Glen Laniel.


After local speakers had addressed
the crowd long preamble and series OF
denunciatory resolutions were read at
the main stand. The features of this
delverance were the endorsement of
the demands of the Paris convention ;
demands for consolidation against capi-
tai statutory establishment of the
eight-hour day; resort to violence to
attain the ends desired, and allegiance
to the Socialistic party.


After the resolutions were read, II.
G. Wiltshire, wealthy Socialist from
Los Angeles, California, addressed the
meeting. He predicted that agitation
for an eight-hour law was only fore
runner to the demand that four hours
should be considered days labor.


The resolutions were adopted with a
whoop, and the affair at the main stand
was over.


On Broadway and Fourth avenue were
trucks filled with Socialist speakers,
who addressed the crowds in various
tongues. Among the speakers was E..
Wissmann, of San Francisco.

Lee Mon Wing, a Chinese cook, stabbed

why? | stabbed her to the heart, all

The heavy rain on the afternoon of
July a was the cause of much excite
ment in Waterbury. A Hebrew dealer
in sponges, with his stock in trade on
his back, WIS walking through the prin-
cipal streets when the shower came on
He was no. dressed in holiday attire, so
he did not mind the rain, but his load of
sponges evidently enjoyed the shower
They swallowed every drop that fell
upon them, and pretty soon they began
to swell. The faster the rain fell the
bigger grew the sponges, until finally
they took up the larger half of the side
walk.


A policeman whose coat sleeve had
been dampened by coming in contact
with the mass of sponges ordered the
man to walk in the middle of the street
He obeyed, but this only made matters
worse. His pack grew larger and larger,
until the peddler looked like gigantic
walking mushroom. Carriage horses
were frightened at the sight, and even
street car horses. which rarely pay atten-
ton to anything but the conductors
signal, turned out for him and drew the
cars off the track. Dogs ran after the
man, and made life miserable for him by
shifting at his heels and barking.


People stood totally oblivious to the
heavy rainfall and laughed until the
tears came. Finally the peddler, still
unconscious Of the trouble, became wor-
ried and a hunted look came into his
eyes. He turned off into side street
and started toward Naugatuck, and the
celebration of the Fourth went on.-An.
sonia Conn. Sentinel.

Centaur.


The British bark Centsur, now at Beale-
street Wharf, had a rough time of it while
off the Horn on the passage to this port.
She rounded the Horn all right, but before
she had gone far was struck by succession
of heavy gales, which drove her far to the
south and east. The weather was intensely
cold and the crew suffered much.


The vessel was hove to nearly two weeks,
and during that time the sea often swept
her decks, and it looked as though she
would have her decks smashed in by the
heavy seas. There was good deal of sick
ness among the crew, some one being on
the sick-list during the whole passage,
while the chief officer was down nearly two
months with rheumatism.


After reaching the equator the Centaur
was becalmed over two weeks. The run Of
hard luck did not leave her when she
reached port, for while lying at anchor in
the stream a day or two ago she was run
into By schooner and the starbOard cat
head taken out Of her.

All men who employ animals in work
know how their speed falls off with
increasing age. Race horses are with
drawn from the track shortly after they
have arrived at the full possession of
their force; they are still good for COM
petitions in bottom, and are capable for
many years yet of doing excellent trot-
ting service, but they cannot run in

Mans capacity to run likewise de-

and the professional couriers who are
still seen in Tunis, running over large
distances in an incredibly short time,
are obliged to retire while still young.
Those who continue to run after they
are forty years old all finally succumb

TowsoSrowS, Nd. October 6. 1891.


Detectives Mahon and Carter of Washington
were here yesterday to give evidence in the
case OF William Jackson and James Brown,
negroes. who were tried for burglary and as
sault The two negroes lived in Virginia just
across the river from Washington. and one was
arrested in Washington, while the other was
captured in Alexandria


The crime was committed on the Path Of
August on the farm of DIR. W. p. Bland. near
Glencoe. They entered the house of Rodney
Scott the foreman on the farm, about 4 o'clock
in the morning and assaulted Mrs. Scott and
left her for dead.


The trial took place in Judge Burke's court
and the prisoners were defended BY colored
members Of the bar. They waived a trial by
jury and after lengthy arguments followed the
testimony the judge announced that his decis-
ion was against them.


The prisoners then asked for mercy but
Judge Burke told them that he could be no
more merciful than the law and reminded
them that they did not show any mercy when
they committed the crime. The judge added
that they were fortunate that the charge
against them was not murder. In giving them
the extent Of the law--ten years in the Balti-
more penitentiary-the judge expressed sor-
row that he could not give them more.


Frank hall, the third negro, who was arrested
In Baltimore, was acquitted.

ington can pass no law for

county, and that the term highway

improvements beyond her Jurisdiction,

the state of Oregon in the construction OF
railroad and cannot loan sr extend its
credit thereto. This settles the ques-
ton of taking joint legisla-
tive action for the relief of the
commerce Of Eastern Washington and
Oregon. The committee will report to the
respective legislatures Monday that moth.
ing can be done.

New YORK, April 23.-Organized Italian
stone-masons to-day caused good deal of
trouble in the upper end of the city. They
struck work to-day in demand for eight
hours time with nine hours pay. President
Gompers of the Federated Trades an
nounced to them that they could easily ac-
complsh their demand. This morning they
went to several houses, and induced some
non-unionists to quit work. Finally they
struck building on One Hundred and
Thirty-fifth street where large numbersof
Italian non-union masons were employed
and they refused to quit. The strikers drew
stilettos and picked up stones and were
about to raid the place when the pon-union
men drew revolvers. The strikers then con-
tented themselves with firing yoleys Of
stones A dangerous riot was imminent
when force of police came up and arrested
dozen of the men. Another small riot was
started few blocks away and more arrests
were made there.

NEW LONDON, June 26.-The sixteenth
annual four-mile eight-oared boat race
between the Yale and Harvard univer-
sity crews was rowed this noon over the
Thames course from Winthrop point to
Gates ferry, and was won by Harvard
in eleven lengths; time, 21:23; Yale's
time, 81 :57.


Harvard's victory was the biggest sur
prise in college athletics for many years.
Good Judges of rowing conceded the race
to Yale almost to a man, and owing to
this sentiment in favor Of Yale, stacks
of money left at the pool rooms went un-
covered, even at odds of 100 to 90.


HARVARD TOOK THE LEAD


at the start and forged ahead with a
rush. AS their shell went ahead, the
crimson supporters on the observation
train and innumerab)e steamers
became frantic with excitement. AS the
excitement spread, some very reckless
work was done by steamboat captains.
That there were two collisions and no
serious results was simply matter OF
good luck. Two miles up the river the
tug boat Gypsy ran into the side OF the
press boat the shock throwing twenty
i've or thirty people off their feet. At
the finish, where the channel was
crowded with all sorts of craft, the press
boat, in trying to avoid collision with
the Rhode Island, struck the tug Amer
lea, knocking many people sprawing
over the deck. Fortunately no one was
injured.


THE SCENES AT THE FINISH


were of most exciting character, the
Harvard men being wild with joy,
while the thousands of Yale supporters
were decidedly crestfallen over their
unexpected defeat. The scenes along
the river were of an unusually brilliant
and lively character. An observation
train of thirty-five cars carried an i'm
mense crowd, while at least seventy
five steamers and steam and sail yachts
followed the crews over the course or

bank was also crowded with sight-seers.


Promptly at IL 80 the crews came
down the river toward che stake boats.
Harvard backed into position minute
late, and the Yales soon after.


PROGRESS OF THE RACE.


When the crews were given the word,
Harvard caught it first, and setting the
fast stroke of forty to the minute at once
pushed the bow of their boat slightly in
front. Yale started with thirty-eight
strokes. For few strokes both crews
caught the swell and splashed quite
badly, then settling down, each crew
gave pretty exhibition OF rowing the
Harvards, however, clearly sending
the boat along at better speed than
they had ever shown in practice, were
gradually creeping away from Yale.
Yale's work on the other hand was
much inferior to that seen in their daily
practice.

the steamers crowded in on the boats
and the swell caused both to do some

the mile flag Harvard increased her lead
to nearly three lengths. From the mile
to the mile and half, Harvard contin-
ued to gain and it became a question by

HARVARD STILL FORGING AHEAD.


In the next half the Harvards, by
strong and steady work, increased their
lead to nearly six lengths. The Yales'
boat continued to settle and hang, and
it was now procession.


Just after passing the navy yard the

course. and they were obliged to make a

the gap between their boat and Yale.


At two and half miles, Harvard had
gained an additional three lengths,
and after passing the three and half
mile flag, they had a good lead of ten
lengths.


THE FINAL Squirt.


Both crews now settled down for the
final spurt, and here again Harvard
showed superiority in every way over
the New Haven crew. Both crews did
excellent work, but the Harvard shell
continued to show steady gam, and
they passed the finish pulling forty
strokes minute, while Yale, eleven
lengths behind, lowed thirty-seven.
The Harvard crew rowed at once to
their quarters, and Yale padded up to
Gates ferry.


The officials were: Referee, William
A. Meikelham, Columbus; judges, Law
renee E. Sexton, Harvard, and Bob

CAUSE OF YALE's DEFEAT.


The cause of Yale's unexpected and
overwhelming defeat, is found IN the
fact that two of her men, the two most
important in the boat, Stroke Gould
and Hagerman, No. 7, were not equal

AS Harvard began to increase their lead

ratified, the result being that for the

tain Brewster. The difference IN
swing OF the men was slight, but enough
to cause Yale's boat to hang perceptlbly
after each stroke, and to settle 80 badly

the water for three or four feet. Both
crews were also greatly annoyed by the
swell from the bigsteamers that followed

A Mate Buried at Sea TOSSED Back on


the Deck by the storm.


The ship Ivy Leaf, Captain Cariin. from
Honolulu to Boston, put into this port late
last night and landed the body of her second
mate, John Simpson, after which she imme-
diately proceeded to her destination.


Simpson was native of Scranton. and it
was his dying wish that his body should be
sent home to his friends. He died on the
2Slh of January of typhoid fefer, and in
accordance with his desire his body was at
once shipped on to Scranton, his friends be-
ing apprlsed by wire of the sad event.


Captain Carlin said TO Philadelphia
Times reporter that this voyage was the
most cventful he had ever seen.


The voyage out was an ordinary one,
with fair winds and no incidenG of any con-
sequence. Immediately the ship left Homo
lulu the trouble began. The first mate was
Scotchman named Hamilton, a tall, strap
ping fellow, who loved his work and never
was known to Shirk it.


While at Honolulu it was noticed that
Hamilton became very respondent. His
bright cheerful disposition left him and he
became morose, surly and petulant.


The crew noticed this and felt sorry, for
the first mate was great feyorite. The
captain called him, and jokingly inquired if
he was in love or sick, but to all the quizzing
of the captain he said nothing. One day.
when about half way between Honolulu
and this port, Hamilton fell sick and was
confined 10 his cabin. The CAPTAIN did all
he could with his scanty stock of medicines
and his limited knowledge to relieve
the suffering man, but without avail, for he
died week after his sickness began. His
death affected the crew in a strange manner !;
the men gathered togenher and whispered
about the strange sounds they had heard in
the hold and the curious nature of the first
mates illness, and all seem oppressed and
weighed down with 4 foreb0dlng of coming
evil.


The mate was buried the day after he died,
in the usual sailor fashion, his bQdy wrapped
in canvas and his feet weighted down with
lead. His burial took place in the morn
ing and the same night storm arose, be-
fore which the vessel had to run under
bare poles. All night the storm ragged
and the captain kept the deck continuously.
About noon the next day Captain Carlin
slapped into the cabin TO get cup of
coffee. He had scarcely sat down when ne
heard loud scream arise above the noise
of The storm. Rushing on deck, he saw the
men huddled together and clinging to the
ropes around the mainmast, looking with
eyes starting from their sockets at an OBJ
ject rolling with the vessel at every lurch.


When the men saw the captain they
pointed to the rolling bundle aud shouted
something, but the noise of the gale
drowned their voices. Creeping toward the
object Captain Carlin watched his chance.
obu, 40 ~ paooSu oclLCu ~, n Wy VI
horror burst from his lips as he saw before
him the face of his dead first officer, whom
he had buried the day previous. The eyes
were wide open, and a smile was still about
the lips


Calling the men to his aid the captain
again sewed the body tightly in canvas and
again consigned it to the sea. The storm al
most Immediately subsidized, aud they had
fair weather the rest OF the voyage.


But their troubles were not ended. Two
days after the second burial of the mate a
seaman named Harrison fell overheard and
was drowned, and the next day the second
officer took sick. Captain Carliu is not by
any means superstitious man, but he can
not and will not attempt to explain the
strange happenings of his voyage.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 4.-The dead
bodies of Sigfried Gosch, German la
borer. his wife and infant son, Willis,
were found at their cottage on the San
Bruno road this morning. Gosch had
evidently aroused his wife from sleep
early in the morning, threatening her
life and those of the children. Her dead
body was found lying across the cradle
of her ten months old child. Her
cheek had been laid open with blow
from hatchet, and her skull had been
cleft by second blow. The infants
clothes were covered with blood. Gosch
then cut his wife's wrists and apparently
attempted to drag her dead body from
the cradle to reach the infant, but chang
ing his mind, turned to his other
sleeping child, who was about 2
years CT age, and crushed in
its skull with another blow of the ham,
mer. He then proceeded to the kitchen
and apparently determined to cut his
throat with razor, but again changed
his mind and proceeded to the yard out
side the house, where he hanged himself
to tree with piece of clothes line.
The bodies we're found this morning by
Mrs. Sternitzky, the aged mother oi
Mrs. Gosch, who was prostrated by the
sight. Gosch had been complaining
some time of his penniless condition,
though doing well for laburer, and his

company report that since the treaty went
into effect they have had to charter three
extra steamers. and every ship has gone out
full. The shipments of machinery for the
manufacture of sugar have been greater than
ever before. A leading provision merchant
In Havana estimates that when the treaty
provision as to the reduction of the duty on
-four takes effect in January next the i'm
ports from the United States TO Cuba will

Mrs. VIM. Grimes Of Guthrie, Okla, after
completing her domestic duties yesterday, laid
down on the bed in her room and went to sleep.
Her four-year-old daughter found box Of
matches and set fire to the window curtains.
The child had previously locked the bedroom
door and thrown the key out of the window.
When the mother awoke the whole room was
ablaze. She could not escape by the door and
was obliged to leap from the window with her
child in her arms Her clothing had caught
fire. and when she fell to the ground she was
wrapped in flames. Neighbors ran to her as
sistance, but were too late to save her life. She
died in terrible agony this morning. Her lit
tie daughter escaped severe injury.

MARYsVILLE. April 1S.-In the Superior
Court to-day Judge Davis rendered very
important opinion relative to the county
printing. Some time ago the Board of Su-
pervisors of YuDa County designated the
Marysville Democrat as the co enty official
paper and fixed the rates of printing. The
Assessor, Tax Collector and other officers
gave their work to the Marysyille Appeal,
which did the printing according to the
rates. The Democrat also published the
same. The Supervisors rejected the Appeals
bill, but allowed the other. The Appeal
then brought suit to recover the amount,
$50 The county demurred on the grounds
that the complaint did not state ground
sufficient for cause of action. Judge
Davis overruled the demurrer. The closing
paragraph is as follows: We have there
fore come to the conclusion that the County
Government Act, intending to furnish COM
plete system 10 the county government,
has suprrs 'ded and repealed Section 4047 of
the Political Code, which empowered Boards
of Supervisors to contract for the county
printing, and that now, under the said act,
after such boards have fixed the price for
such printing, each county officer may pro-
cure such printing as his Office by law re-
quires, at the prices so fixed, from any per-
son he may elect to deal with, subject to the
restrictions imposed by said subdivision 90,
and that such work Will be a legal charge
against the county"

the Justices Court to the Superior Court of

William Boden and his brother George are

morning they appeared at the Office Of Sanitary

THEIR STRAIGHTFORWARD STORY.
Their story was that they were here on their
way home from Jacksonville, Fla, where their
father took them four or i've months ago.
The elder Of the brothers said that his father
was divorced from his mother at jamestown
some months ago. and that he went to Florida,
taking with him three children, sister thirteen
years old and themselves.


Before leaving jamestown he said his father
visited lady there and after reaching Jackson
vile he (William) had an idea that his father
was going to get married. He did not have the
courage to speak to his father such a sub
ject, but one day he sat down and wrote him a
long letter advising him against the marriage.





course did not take his advice, and mar
ried the lady, who was widow with q
seventeen-year daughter. The chill
dren all got along nicely together, his sister
and stepsister working about the house to-
gether until one day when the stepsister
found the letter spoken of and then there was
trouble. The boys said that from that time
their lives were made unhappy and finally they
went to their father and told him that they
could stand it no longer and were going back
to jamestown.


THE FATHER SAYS "Go."


His answer to them, they said, was '"Then
60" They did as he said and left. Having no
money they tramped sixty miles to another
town, where they told their story to lawyer,
and the kind-hearted man made up purse for
them and put them on the train. The conductor
passed them through a long way and then they
paid their fare to this city. Sanitary Officer
Frank sent them to the Newsboy's Home where
they were kindly cared for by Agent Sweeny,
who gave them each new overcOat and other
clothing. He questioned the boys separately

ground and was dragged away by his COM
panions. BY this time everything was in an
uproar. Women screamed and O mad rush for
the exits was made

knocked down and trampled on. The manager
OF the show got on a stand and attempted to
quiet the mob with speech but it was useless.
and he, like the clown, was knocked down.
At this point the riot spirit took command.
Everything in sight was seized and wrecked.
The band instruments were smashed fat The
seats were torn down and broken. Some one
cut the ropes and the big tent came down with
a sudden rush, burying 200 or more people in
its folds.


Arush was then made for the dressing rooms.
which we're also torn down, leaving the actors
and actresses half dressed in the open air. The
side shows were next attacked and were
wrecked. After wrecking everything in sight
the crowd went away and the show people,
aided by the police, gathered their traps to-
gether and left on a midnight train. Some
twenty persons were hurt, but none seriously.
except the clown, whose nose was broken and
lower jaw fractured.

TWIN SISTERS have been brought to
Paris from Bohemia that have excited
the interest of the medical faculty. They
are not joined together by mere iga-
ture like the Siamese brothers, but are
united at the lower part of their bodies.
They have two stomachs and distinct
tastes. Josepha made up her mind that
she would not take wine again after
having experienced illness from it,
whilst Rosa insists on indulging in the
beverage, to the great disgust of the
other who gets angry because she has
to go to bed to let her sister sleep off
the bad effects of her dissipation. They
are fourteen years of age, and are con-
sidered great natural curiosity, as they
are pretty, good tempered and amiable,
whilst each has tastes and desires diff
ferent from the other.

Blue eyes are soft as summer skies,
In their sweet depths bright Cupid nes;
They speak of love, Of truth and grace,
kindly heart and smiling face
That bashful innocence possess;
With glorious power they seen to bless
The love which you on them bestow.
The hazel eye, with luster bright,
Shines with CLEAN Of winning light,
Like the gazelles, with softest power,
They'll WOO you to their Eden bower:
They're filed with loves enchanting song,
To cheer life's dreary course along;
They've conquered worlds; orbs man frst saw
In Paradise, then broke Gods law.
Gray eyes command by cold disdain;
The intellectual they retain;
Now Hash with anger, wit or scorn,
Brave as great Mars. but cold as morn;
With naughty look, imperial pride,
Loves passion they can surely hide;
Though they may feel its gentle sway
They'll hide from you its heavenly say.
While eyes of black. all liquid fire,
Consumed by passion or desire
Burn like lamp, with love divine;
But jealous, like the serpent's shine:
They're all on fire with PASSIONS power;
They'll love and hate within an hour;
will die to shield the one loved best,
But wronged, will dagger his vile breast
mixture OF the two extremes,
The naughty gray, the blacks fierce beams,
Show iife's great course in different forms,
Through fowery paths, or darkest stormA
But when the hazel twines with blue,
What happy scenes present TO view;
The noble, generous, wise and good
Have all within their portals stood.

There was an exciting fight in the Watson
Beasley household, in Ridge street alley, about
O'Clock yesterday morning, which resulted in
the wounding of Allen Watson and his wife,
Charlotte, and Aliens stepson, Squire Beasley.
Besides the large quantity Of blood that was
spilled much noise was made and the whole
neighborhood was aroused. The house is in
the rear of No. 440 N street and is occupied
only by the one family. Charlotte has three
grown children, one son and two daughters,
but they were not at home Saturday night
until late hour. When they arrived they
found that Allen, who was under the influence
Of liquor, had beaten their mother. Squire,
who just recovered from the effects of a shot
in the leg, took his mothers part, and then it
was that the most serious part Of the trouble
occurred. Squire's mothers head was badly
cut and soon after that wound was inflicted
Squire was cut several times by his stepfather,
who had a razor. He was cut about the
shoulder and collar bone, but in the fight he
did not forget to defend himself and one
thing he did in that direction was to strike the
old man on the head and infiict wound which
will make him remember the fight for some
time Officer Trammell Of the second precinct
appeared at the house before the blood had
been cleared away and put an end to the
domestic difficulty by arresting Allen and lock-
ing him up. The lamp which Squire struck
his stepfather with was broken in thousand
pieces, which were scattered on the floor.
Squire and his mother walked all the way to
the Emergency Hospital, where DIR. Hall
dressed their wounds and they then returned
home.


When Judge Miller heard the case this morn
ing and the testimony was given it was shown
that the old woman did the first fighting and
that Watson, who was crowded to the wall,
acted entirely in self defense, and he was
therefore discharged.

A tramp whose name is not known here
went into the saloon of James Clancy

hands. The marshal arrested the tramp,
who was put in Jail.

several hundred persons visited the jail,
overpowered the sheriff, took out the pris-
oner and hung him to telegraph pole.
There is no clue whatever of the identity
OF the tramp.

The new tariff bill, which admits sugar,
molasses, coffee, tea and hides, raw and
uncured, free, provides that if the gov
eminent of any country producing and
exporting such articles shall, after the first
day of January, 1892, impose duties or
other exactions upon the agricultural or
other products of the United States,
which duties are reciprocally unjust,
the president of the United States
shall have the power and it shall
be his duty to suspend the provisions of
the act admitting the sugars, molasses,
tea, coffee and hides of such country free.
So that after the first of next year the ports
OF the United States will be practically
closed to the nations of this continent
whose sense of justice does not lead them
to remove discriminating duties on the
agricultural products of the United States.


Brazil, the greatest of the South Ameri-
can republics, has already complied with
the requirements of the tariff law. and
will, on and after April /, 1891, admit free
Of duty American agricultural products,
coal and machinery, while the duty On
lumber, meat products, canned goods, cot
ton cloth and furniture will be reduced
one.fourth. This will practically give the
United States a monopoly of the Brazilian
trade. Cuba and Venezuela are about to
open their ports to American farm pro-
ducts and manufactures, and every other
Spanish-American country must follow.
The United States will be without a COM
petitor in the greatest market in the world.


The far-reaching craftsmanship of James
6. Blaine is now apparent. The tariff bill
originally contained no provision COM
polling nations whose products were adj
mitted into the United States free of duty
10 return the favor. Blaine, against the
opposition of the Democrats and some of
his own party, but, however, strongly
supported by the president, compelled the
insertion of the reciprocity clause.


The farmers of the United States are
|. now given foreign market. This meas
ure for their relief seems much more
effective than the plan proposed by Sock
less Jerry Simpson and the whiskered SEN
ator Pfeifer, OF Kansas, that the govern
ment build warehouses in which the farm
ers may deposit wheat and pumpkins and
borrow money from the national treasury
thereon.


Reciprocity is Republican doctrine The
Democrats proposed 10 open our market to
those nations which would buy nothing
from us, and whose tariffs excluded our
productions.

CHICAGO, August 26.-A dispatch from San
Francisco says: Advices from Singapore state
that the steamer Namchow sailed from that
port with 500 Chinese coolies for the Penang
market. The officers were Chinese. with the
exception of half dozen Europeans While
at sea cholera broke out among the Chinese
The sick crowded in the cabins, where a Pres
byterian minister and one lady passenger had
taken refuge. After a terrible hurricane the
CHOLERA continued to spread and deaths be-
came very numerous. At first each victim was
cast into the sea with bar Of pig iron in the
sack Soon, however, the dead were mostly
thrown overheard without ceremony. The
death roll grew alarming, and no less than
sixty bodies were thrown into the sea. The
supercargo had supreme control and insisted
upon heaving overheard all effects Of the dead
Under threats the captain upon arrival at Singa-
pore reported only six deaths to the harbor
master, three from influenza and three from
want of opium and general debility" Many
passengers were landed and no quarantine being
declared proceeded to Penang with the rest
OF the infected cargo and crew. In four days
nine cases Of cholera developed in Singapore,
all traced to the steamer Namchow. On the
steamers voyage back from Penang, after
landing 200 coolies. the first European victim,
the third engineer, an Engllshman, succumbed
to the terrible disease. When tho Namchow
arrived at Singapore the health officer was on
the lookout and sent the vessel into quaran-
tine. When the vessel is released the captain
and supercargo will be arrested and placed on
trial at Singapore.

SAN Francisco, Feb. 27.-Dispatches
received by the railroad officials from
Yuma. today, say that every building
in town except the Southern Pacific
hotel and the penitentiary, have been
destroyed by the food. Last night the
Gila and Colorado rivers rose thirty
three feet above low water mark. The
passenger and freight depots were both
flooded, and the water rose to level
with the bridge across the Colorado
river. In order to prevent the bridge
from being carried away by the freight
depot being set afloat, the building was
blown up with dynamite. This morn
ing the river dropped seventeen inches
in one hour, and the Yuma residents
are feeling less anxious. All the country
eastward for twenty miles is under
water, and the Southern Pacific tracks
are washed out for fully that distance.
Trains are running between Ell Paso and
Tucson, but westbound passengers are
held at Tucson.


THE FLOOD AT IT'S HEIGHT.


YUMA, Ariz., Feb. 27.-The water
reached the highest point at II O'Clock
last night. Every business house is
washed down. The convent OF st. Jo-
seph, the A. 0. U. w. hall, the express
and telegraph offices and the postoffice
are leveled to the ground. The railroad
and steamboat Office was swept into the
Colorado river. The railroad ice house
and the track at the foot of Main street
have been washed away. Five hundred
men worked last night to save property,
but met with little success. The town
and property are now guarded by men,
bers of the Yuma rifles, who have been
sworn in as deputy sheriffs. The water
is now falling here, but reports of further
rises have been received from above and
east which, if correct, will entirely
sweep Yuma away. The railroad both
ways is impossible.


THE GILA RISING AGAIN,


CLIFTON, Ariz., Feb. 27.-The river has
risen again. Property is destroyed--
roads demolished, dams and fumes
gone. Work has been suspended by
both the Arizona and Detroit copper
mining companies. The south approach
to the iron bridge here, and the entire
iron bridge at Guthrie, twelve miles
south, are gone. 1t is Impossible to es-
innate the damage now. This report
was sent on a handcar to Duncan, thirty
eight miles south. Extravagant reports
OF the destruction OF farms in the Gila
valley have been received.

A peculiar and fatal accident hap
pened recently to man named Dun
ham who lived in Kechi township, Sedg-
wick County, Kan. A farmer named
Martin had killed number of hogs,
which he left hanging in his yard over
night. In the morning one was gone,
and in looking around for some trace
which might reveal the cause of its dis
appearance, he noticed, a short distance
from his house, something strange
propped against rail fence, and on in
vestigating found his hog hanging by
the gambrel stick around the neck of
Dunham.


The thief's neck was broken, and he
had evidently been dead some hours.
The supposition is that while climbing
the fence Dunham's burden had slipped
and caught his head in the moose formed
by the two legs and the cross stick, and
the heavy weight had instantaneously
cracked his neck.-Kansas City Star.

Lightning Strikes Camp OF Grand Army


Men and Sons Of Veterans.


During severe rain storm at Grand Island,
Neb., yesterday. where the state Grand Army
and Sons of Veterans reunion is being held, a
lightning bolt struck the camp. Two ieuten-
ants and four sergeants of cavalry troop K
were seated in the first sergeant's tent. The
lightning struck the tent, scattering the splin-
tiers in all directions. Nine men were struck.
When the alarm was given the two lieutenants
and four sergeants were found lying fiat in the
tent with their heads buried in the debris. The
guards were found lying on the ground. The
doctors believe that all will recover.


The tent was wrecked, and it is believed that
had it not been for the metal on the pole many
people in the surrounding tents would have
been killed. On the arms and legs Of the in.
jured there appear great knots, produced by
the electric fluid. The injured men are suffer
ing intense pain, but their comrades are doing
all in their power to relieve their sufferings.

by HOusebreakers.


Mrs Gretchen Lenzenhagen and her if
teen-year-old son George were found dead in
the formers saloon at 444 South Clark street
Chicago, yesterday morning. The woman
was choked to death by unknown robbers, who
then beat and choked the boy until life left
his body. The robbers forced open
the till in the saloon and ransacked
the drawers behind the bar. The three living
rooms Of the woman in the rear of the saloon
also showed signs of the work of the murder
ers. The bed clothing was torn from the beds.
drawers were from the bureau and the contents
scattered all over the floor. Everything which
was capable of concealing any valuables was
thoroughly ransacked.


Mrs. Lenzenhagen and her son lived alone
and made but few intimate acuuaintances,
but the woman had frequently expressed her
lack Of confidence in banks and it was COM
monty rumored around the neighborhood that
she had considerable wealth secreted about the
premises. The woman was last seen when she
closed her saloon shortly before midnight The
police are endeavorins to find out who were
her last customers and expect that they will
soon have some definite clue to the per-
petrators.

morning with Captain Parker and five

by and five Of the crew are reported

Butler left Port Gamble November 2Sth,

take to the boats on the 9th
inst. Their haste was 30 great that

100 miles off shore, but the force OF the
gale was such, that 1T was three days be-
fore those in Captain Parker's boat
could land, and the sufferings from
hunger and exposure were great.
