EVANSVILLE, Feb. 9. - Yesterday be-
tween 1880 O'Clock in the forenoon and 4
o'clock in the afternoon the railroad ticket
office was entered and $3.50 taken. The
thief unlocked the outside and inside office
doors and turned the combination on the
safe. The burglar-box had not been locked
The thief opened it and took about $780,
leaving $3.50 check, $50 wrapped in paper
and some small coins. There were no marks
of violence, and the work was evidently
done by man familiar with the surround
ings. Agent Baird left the office at 1890
o'clock and did not return until o'clock
He found the safe-dOor open and the money
gone, but everything else in good order.
All the other employees went to Woodland
on an excursion. Baird says it is his per-
sonal loss, as he should have locked the
burGlar-box. Much mystery surrounds the
case and he and the police have no idea
who the culprit is. Baird has been agent
here for twenty years, and during that time
the safe has been tapped three times, but
unsuccessfuly. About one year ago the
office was entered and fine revolver taken,
but nothing else was disturbed.


Marysville has been overrun with swim
ders, burglars and murderers since the
opening of the recent citrus fair. Nearly
all the work is done by travelling men.
Only two captures have been made-one
for burglary and one for robbery. The
cGlprits were sent to tile State Prison for six

Honduras and the Legislature.


NEW YORK. Sept. 25.-The Star and Her
aid publishes the following account of the
difficulty at Balize, British Honduras. be-
tween the Administration and the LegisIa-
ture. After protracted struggle between
the Government and the popular eIe-
ment of the Legislature, not unlike
that between Balmaceda and the Chilean
Congress, the Representatives vacated their
seats in body. The Governor, in no way
disconnected, promptly appointed in their
room certain officials whom he designated
unofficial" members, inasmuch as they did
not occupy their seats eX-Officio. There was
at that time, February last no one to
gainsay him, and from February to
July the colony was practically run
under a Balmacedan form of govern.
ment. An action was laid in July against
the Collector of Customs to recover alleged
illegally exacted duties, on the ground that
the Colony possessed no Constitutional
Legislature, either at the present time or
when the new tariff was voted. The
Government went into court and defended
itself. Chief Justice Anderson was in a
quandary for precedents, but finally gave
judgment for plaintiffs, thereby oyerruling
the Legislature and annulling ali laws
passed since February. The Government
has appealed to the Privy Council.

= San SALVADOR, Sept. 9.-Millions of
dollars worth of property and many
lives were destroyed in this republic by
an earthquake today. Whole towns
were wiped out, and SO far as the adj
vices received indicate hardly city in
the country, except those along the
coast, escaped the awful effects of the
convulsion.


There had been indications for several
days past that seismic disturbance of
more than usual power might be ex-

morning the earth began to shake. The
wave had strong vertical and oscil-
latory movement. The people rushed

and while the shock lasted only twenty
seconds, before it passed away there was
q pdulC-SJTlChen LuOU ludhIuS lLS way 10

Men, women and children were shrek
ing and praying in the streets.


The walls of houses cracked, tottered
and fell. There was deep continuous
rumbling, as of heavy thunder. The
earth rose and fell in long waves, and
the people were unable to keep their
feet.


All through the morning there had
been slight shocks, but none approaching
in intensity that which was SO destruc-
tive.


President Ezetais doing everything he

is feared many people were killed in the
smaller towns.

San Francisco, Aug. e.-Further details OF the
-reat earthquake and tidal wave at the mouth OF
the Colorado River show that the first reports
were not exaggerated. Jose Perez, cattleman
from Lerdo, has reached Yuma He says that
on the forenoon of the day of the earthquake
several men were building fences on his place
when suddenly the fence toppled over. All
threw themselves on their knees and began pray
ing In the midst of their devotions hundred
foot tidal wave showed up The prayers were
cut short, and, jumping over an unexpected
crevasse in the roadway, the Andrade hill was
reached by the men. From that peak Perez states,
tbe sight was sublime. Across the Colorado turbu-
lent volcanoes could be seen in brilliant eruption.
On the bed of the river and some miles beyond
its banks reddish -colored, fOam-covered water
rushed ahead, at the height of fully 100 feet.
Below Lerdo could be seen wide river of blush
purple fire flowing down into the Colorado near
the Gulf, where it steamed, sputtered and added
10 the general confusion. Ihis river oil nre Is
undoubtedly from Sulphur Mountain, which, 1t Is
feared, has been set on fire from the volume OF
burning and infammable material thrown out
from the volcanoes, which heretofore have never
been known 10 throw out anything but mud and
hot water.


General Andrade head of the Lerdo colony has
received private advices from the scene OF the
earthquake. He says the force of the shock was
severe, and was much more so than was at first re-
ported One of the largest houses In the colony
was cracked from top 10 bottom, and the roof fell
in with crash that sounded like dynamite blast.
Luckily, the inmates ran out when they felt the
premonitory shake, and thus escaped death. A
large stoble. built partly of brick and partly of
adobe, was levelled TO the ground, and several
other buildings were more or less severely dam
aged The most striking phenomenon was a
chasm three feet wide and between 200 and 300
feet long Although weights attached to lines
several hundred feet in length were let down, no
bottom could be found. From this remarkable
fssure issued smoky vapor, which disappeared
after a few hours but the air is permeated with a
gaseous odor irritating to the lungs. The people
in the neighborhood are alarmed, fearing rcpet-
ton of the earthquake, and the superstitious In
dians are holding religious rites to placate the
Evil One.


Yuma, A. T., Aug o-Reports continue TO come
In from the earthquake region at the head Of the
Gulf of California. Two Cocopah Indians, of
the tribe that live near there, arrived here yes
terday They tell thrilling story. Early Thurs
day morning hundreds of mud volcanoes thirty
miles of burst into violent eruption. The
air grew denser and many infants were suGocated.
At last a violent thunder storm cleared the air.
only to show the tidal wave approaching with
frightful rapidity. The waters rose swallowing
up their cattle, horses and grain fields and driv-
ing them for their lives TO the top of the mesas
a hundred feet above the river. The earthquake
shocks then began. The fourth shock threw
every one down, seriously injuring many. The
dust darkened the air. The rumble of the earth
quake. the sharp explosions of the distant vol
canoes, the bell6wing of the crazed cattle, made
unbearable the uproar, and the frightened Indians
led wildly up the river Two only succeeded in
reaching here, who tell the story. The others
dropped exhausted along the route.

WASHINGTON, July 14.-Further tests
OF American armor plate were made at
the Annapolis proving ground last Sat
urday with gratifying results. Two
three-inch all steel plates were
prepared by Carnegie, with
surfaces treated by the new Harvey
process. To give the process complete
test under better conditions than here
tofore realized, the plates were made
with less carbon in their composition
than the three plates tested some
months ago. The official report has not
yet been received, but the officers pres
ent say the plates satisfactorily stood
the fire from seven-pound Hotchkiss
rifle during six tests.

Great as have been some men who died
young, who knows how much greater
they would have been had their lives
been prolonged. Might not Marlowe
have rivaled Shakespeare? Yet possibly
Byron had already given us his best,
and Shelley and Keats might not have
surpassed their early efforts.


Had the author of ''Festus' died at 90
there would have been lamentation as
over Keats, but Bailey has lived half a
century longer without producing Sec
ond poem. Tasso, though he lived TWEEN
ty years after Jerusalem Delivered" !"
never equaled that epic, written at 81


Still there are men whose longevity
has certainly stood for much. Michael
Angelo showed astonishing precocity.
but he owes to his eighty-nine years his
great renown as painter, sculptor and
sonneteer. Voltaire's fame, again, rests
on the entirety of his writings, not on
any single work, and the literary dicta-
torship with which age invested him.
Cut off twenty years of his life, and his
fame would perceptibly shrink. Goethe,
Emerson, Carlyle, Longfellow, Tenny-
son, Hugo, Dumas-all had the advan-
tage of fullness of years, so as to be
judged by bulk as we'll as quality. Hum
boldt, too, owed to his ninety years a
portion of his reputation.


The true comparison would obviously
be between works produced at the same
age, or between men dying at about the
same age, but it is much easier to test
achievement than capacity. Perhaps the
best books Gin posse) have never been
written, and we often feel that the men
were greater than their works. Who
knows, moreover, what geniuses have
died in childhood Monthly.

CHICAGO, April 5.-A murderous fight,
the result of long standing feud, be-
tween two italian women, Mrs. Jesse
Gallo and Mrs. Congetto Vallone. oc-
CURED tonight in State-street tene-
ment house. Mrs. Vallone called on
Mrs. Gallo, on invitation OF the latter.
to settle matters amicably. As Mrs. Val
lone was taking off her shawl, Mrs. Gal
lilo locked the door, placed the key in
her pocket. went to closet, secured a
large butcher knife, and then coolly in
formed her visitor that she had invited
her for the purpose OF settling their
trouble in true Italian fashion. Mrs.
Vallone attempted to escape, but
her frenzied assailant pitilessly
bore her down upon the floor. Fourteen
times the Gallo woman plunged the
keen blade into her victims neck, face
and body, and only desisted in her
bloody work, apparently from sheer ex-
haustion. The furniture was overturned
and broken and the walls and ceiling
spattered with blood. The police at
this juncture broke open the doors, and
as the officers approached Mrs. Gallo
rushed upon them with the bloody
knife still clenched tightly in her hand.
A fierce struggle ensued, but the desper-
ate woman was overpowered and her
victim taken to the hospital. Mrs. Val
lone cannot recover. Mrs. Gallo was
held without bail.

age only. Many suits resulted, acre tract

Father Filmanof, an Orthodox Russian
priest in the province of Kasan describes thus
his visit to the starving village of Naredey:


I'm the first half hour l met sixteen persons
in the death struggle. An old woman died be
fore my eyes. Most of the starving persons
had not tasted bread for eight days. White
faced, blear-eyed, the stricken men stared
helplessly at me. They have lost even the
strength required to stretch out their hands in
mute petition for bread. Only the most for
tunate have their prayer granted; the rest die
before help can arrive. Before the houses on
the curbs, at the church door and the market
place saw the pale. haggard, bent and dis
eased figures. Every look meant hunger AMI
weakness. Some crept along in apparent in
difference and resignation; others acted as il
mad, and cried: Bread! Bread! Don't let us
die -


'The mothers whose children have already
succumbed to hunger lament day and night
Everything edible has been consumed. So
long as there were weeds and berries life was
possible. but when these were gone all felt
themselves face to face with death. In their
despair they stripped the leaves from the lin
dens, dried and ground them and made them
into porridge. This concoction stilled the
pain for about fourteen days. but afforded little
nourishmen.. Then the lindens were stripped
bare and the people began to die. Starvation
makes such rapid ravages hereabouts that
within eight days in one village of $50 families
forty-seven families have died out entirely"

BERLIN, Nov. 14.-The case of Mrs. Catherine
Robinson and Miss Ida Green, who have been
suing for the estate of the late Baron Won Bar
nekow, has been decided in favor of the claim
ants. The court decided that Miss Green is
entitled to call herself Baroness Won Barnekow,
and receive the whole of the barons property
after his debts are paid. Years ago Baron
Won Barnekow, an officer of the German
army, after defalcation fed to America, and
after varied career became runner for a hotel
in San Francisco under the alias of Fred Green.
While employed in this capacity he became ac-
quainted with girl named Galligan. The
couple lived together, though not legally mar
ried, but after the birth OF daughter, the baron
yielded to the Importantly of the girl and
married her, thereby, under the laws of Cali
fornia, making the daughter, though born out
of wedlock, his legal issue. The baron soon re-
sumed his dissipated life, neglecting his family,
and finally deserting them. His wife applied
for and was granted divorce.
Baron Won Barnekow subsequently re-
turned to Germany, falling heir to
the family title and estates. without
obtaining a divorce, he married again in 1887,
the year before his California wife obtained her
divorce. His second marriage was naturally
Illegal Without knowing her husband was
dead Mrs. Green obtained divorce and later
on married sailor named Robinson. After
the baron's death his sister, Countess
Won Moltke, wife of major in the army, and
a near relative of the field marshal, suspecting
the truth, instituted search which resulted
in finding the former wife and child OF the
baron, and led to the establishment of their
claims as legal heirs to the large though heav-
lily encountered estate.
headline: Ida Green Becomes . Baroness.

stand hot climates, dust cloak, travelling
hood and plenty of wraps Three hats for

for the voyage, a jacket aud an ulster
areneeded, and also two or three cool dresses.

ton or zephyrs, as dampness does not affect

couple of ball dresses for evening recep-

ing habit, stylish silk dress, home-spun

portmRnteaus, one for the light weight, the

escape on her to Aspiuwall. The officers at

escape by swimming TO the shore. The officers
noticed this, however, and fired on him in the
water. The shots were well directed and the

meath the waves. Another of the bandits was
captured. The loss to the policemen was light

One of the most remarkable young wom-
en- of the time is Cynthia M. Westover,
secretary of Street Commissioner Beattie,
of New York city. In variety of accom-
plishments there is scarcely her equal any
where among women. Her father was a
geologist and expert miner, and the child
learned to ride almost before she could
walk. She rode with her father all through
the western mountain and mining regions
from Mexico to the Canada line in his pros
pecting journeys. During these years the
child became an expert shot and horse
woman, and learned the Spanish language
besides.


Once, when little girl, she shot dead an
Indian who had his tomahawk uplifted
over the head of white woman. Again,
when her fathers camp was surrounded
by hostile Indians, she galloped out upon
her pony and brought relief. The redskins
saw her, but they were used to meeting the
child riding about after the COWS and did
not disturb her. She had played many
time with the little Indian children and
thus won the good will of the older ones


These years were the making of Cynthia
Westover. They gave her health, practical
knowledge and splendid Independence and
self reliance. She was so much at home
with the shy wild creatures of the wood
that she learned their calls, and they came
to her like domestic birds and animals.

SAN Francisco, Sept. 5.-Today q

trace of the robbers which he had fol-
lowed south from Ceres. Cunningham,
himself did not send this telegram, but
forwarded it by messenger to New
man. His location at the time he sent

Newman was the nearest telegraph

The searching parties that went out

reached La Grange, where the inn

attention of their comrades. A railroad
officer says, in his opinion, the robbers
walked along the track to Modesto, four

train to San Francisco. They might
easily have done so.


No word has been received at the rail-

Smith, nor at Wells, Fargo & Co.'S

tective force that is after the Ceres train

lors. Those leading the chase are
Sheriff Cunningham, Deputies Stockiard

eight hours have passed since the at
tempted robbery, these brave men have
not taken any rest, going night and
day. *
Detective Lawson, this morning, said ::
"At our meeting today we all agreed
that Bob and Emmett Dalton, who are
now at large, the men who figured in
the Alila train robbery, had something
to do with this. The Daltons are ell
acquainted with the country people
here, and it will be hard to convict them
if arrested.


Lawson brought tramp to town this

his name as Colclough, gave the detec-
tive good description of the short man

thinks he could identify him if he saw
him. The officers are confident they
will cage their game within week.

three carriages, loaded with excur-

WASHINGTON, April 8.-The proposed
treaty with Newfoundland, the suspen-
sion of the negotiations regarding which
was ordered from Great Britain because
of the protest of the Canadians, was
made public today. 1t provides that
United States fishing vessels entering
Newfoundland waters, shall have the
privilege of purchasing bait on the
same terms as Newfoundland ves-
sells; also trading without any
charge other than the dues levied
on Newfoundland vessels. The
products of the fisheries of New
foundland shall be admitted free into
the United States; also the packages in
which they are carried. "Green" cod
fish are excepted from this. Duties are
also provided upon flour, rice, salted
meats, etc., imported into Newfound-
lard from the United States. Agricul-
tural implements and machinery, raw
cotton, broomcorn, gas engines, printing
presses and types shall be admitted free
when imported from the United States.


This convention was to take effect as
soon as the bills required to carry it into
operation should have been passed on
each side, and was to remain in force
five years from the time it came into
operation, and further until the ex-
piration of twelve months after either of
the high contracting parties had given
notice to the other of wish to termin-
ate the same.

miles east of Sable Island during a dense fog

were trolling for halibut.

o'clock Saturday night

For the last two months two white women

visited a cabin outside of town. Investigation

night They refused to heed the warning. which
was accompanied by threats of whipping.
About o'clock Friday morning a party of
about thirty men went to the cabin. They ap-
preached quietly, and then rush was made
for the door, which was carried from its hinges.
The inmates were quickly overpowered, led
outside, stripped to the waist and bound to
trees. The thirty men took turns in hogging
the barred backs with a blscksnake whip, every
stroke bringing blood.

each, when they tainted from pain. The men
took the terrible punishment better and were
given q larger dose. After the women re-
gained consciousness they and the two men
were allowed to return to the cabin and dress.
Then they started north on the railroad track.

'NEoCENE AND PLEIsToCENE CONTINENT MOVE


MENrs."


The communication was based on observa-
tions begun in the District Of Columbia some
years since and gradually extended over tho
coasted lowlands from New York through
Florida to the Mississippi river. Mr.. MCGEE
pointed out that by means of these studies he
asccrtained that during past periods the land
stood sometimes higher and sometimes lower
than now with respect to sea level, and during
the past few months the character and ampli-
tude of these continental oscillations have been
ascertained. The record presented before the
session began with the time biologists called
pleistocene, when the land stood from three to
eight hundred feet lower than now. Imme-
diately after this episode the land rose from
height and the shores of the Atlantic and gulf
retreated 500 to 100 miles beyond their present
position. Afterward the land gradually sank
and the waters readvanced until the geography
was much the same as that Of today. Then
came another incursion OF the ocean and gulf
upon which Washington was built and over
considerable portions Of the coastal lOwlands
toward the north and the south. During this
period there was deposited a series OF loans
and brick clay and boulder beds, upon which
Washington was located and which has been
named, from the District, the Columbia forma-
ton. At the close Of the Columbia period
the land again rose 100 or 400 feet
higher than at present and river channels were
cut fifty to seventy-fve miles beyond the present

The officers then arrested two leaders Of the
procession and started with them to the city
hall. Some one III the crowd yelled out. ''Shall
eral shout Of mo, No." and the students,

the policemen.

A desperate conflict ensued. The two stu
dents under arrest were rescued several times.
but refused to escape and were retaken by the
officers. The fight ragged for nearly
hour. Clubs freely used and the
policemen drew their reyolvers when
a mob of Bohemians and saloon
keepers came to their rescue. The students
were then put to fight. One of their number,
Ward Bannister had his head broken open and
was otherwise dangerously injured by blows
from a club. Several others were hurt more
or less seriously.


THE STUDENTS RELEASED.


Within ten minutes after the city hall was
reached an order was secured from the mayor
demanding the police to rele ase the two stu
dents under arrest. The order was ignored
and it became necessary for the marshal to take
the students out. Their preliminary hearing
was postponed until Wednesday owing TO the
excitement existing. The city is much stirred
up over the trouble, and further violence is
feared. The general feeling is that the police
men were wrong.

BRIDGEPoRT, CAL, June 10.-A few
weeks ago Walker river Indian, of the
Piute tribe, named Poker Tom, came
here and purchased some calico and
spent two nights gambling with China
men. The second night was spent at
All Tia's store, and that was the last
seen of Tom. On the 1st of June dele
CATION of Indians from the Walker river
reservation, and Bodie and other Indians
came here looking for him, and stated
that his horse had reached home with
out saddle or bride. A search resulted
in both being found together, with the
calico purchased by Poker Tom, in the
fields north of town. The river was
fished for his body, but none was recov-
cred, though a reservation overcoat was
found on one of the banks.


The Indians ther eupon summoned all
the Indians of their neighborhood to
hold court, suspicion fixing itself upon
All Tia as the cause of Toms disappear
.ance. The Chinaman denied having
PLAYED cards with Poker Tom, but five
Indians testified to having gone to All
Tia's store on the night in question, and
being unable to enter on account of the
door being locked, they looked through
a hole in the window curtain and saw
the Chinaman and Indian Tom playing
cards.


On the following day, when the court
reconvened, the wife of one of the Mono
Indians, known as Lundy, testified that
Lundy, Mono Tom and three other In
dians were intoxicated on the day in
question, and that they must have killed
Poker Tom. Although it was ascertained
that Lundy had left his wife for
some reason, and that she had been
consorting with All Tai, SO that it was
inferred by some that the latter had in
duced her to testify in his behalf, the
Walker river Indians threatened to pro-
ceed against the Mono lake Indians, and
stated that they would have Sheriff
Cody take Lundy and Mono Tom to the
state prison, while they were going to
kill old jim, Lundy's father, and Toms
father, in order to get even.


The Indians, however, discovered that
All Tai had been industriously scrub
bing his floor at place where certain
stains were, and on examination these
were found to be blood stains. Sheriff
Cody also found bullet hole through
one of the walls, and stains covered by
new wall paper, which All Tai declared
were caused by red ink.


On Saturday Poker Toms body was
discovered in the river by some Indians
who were fishing. His head and arms
had been cut off, and also his legs. His
body was sawed open from the neck to
the pit of his stomach. The Indians
became greatly excited, and All Tia was
hastily conveyed to jail at his own re-
quest, to prevent their lynching him. An
inquest has been held, and from a con-
fession by the Chinaman, the jury has
brought in verdict charging All Tia
with murder. The case has aroused
great interest here, and the progress Of
the examination has been eagerly
watched,

Illinois Central, Michigan Central,
Baltimore and Ohio, Big -Four, Grand
Trunk, Wabash, Santa Fe, Lake Shore,
Pan Handle, Burlington, Alton, Rock
Island, the Pittsburg, Fort Wayne and
Chicago, the Eastern Illinois and the
Erie. The exposition management will
assume all obligations for the grounds
over which the tracks pass. The right
of way win furnish room for four tracks,
beginning at the intersection of the Bal

speculators, for an excellent wheat crop

equal distribution of rain have beer
most favorable for the probabilities Of

been sufficient rain in both the Sacra-
mento and San Joaquin valleys, and the
probabilitiet are that the crop will
be as heavy as any had for
some time. Prices are good and the
market is firm. This market, of course,
follows the European market to great
extent, and that market is strong on ac-
count of the failure of the French CROP"


William Dresbach thought that the

STOCKTON, March 7.-Joseph Brunson, a
laboring man, agei 50 years, who had
lived in Lodi sixteen years, committed
suicide at his home early this morning by
cutting his throat with a razor. lie leaves
six children. the eldest being % years aud
the youngest years old. Leonard Brun-
son, a son, aged 10 years, went into the
kitchen at Z o'clock this morning to make
fire and found his father lying on his back
OH the floor His throat was cut, there being
cash on either side. Between his knees
lay razor half closed and covered with
blood. The body was not yet cold, indicat-

hour before. Dependency over the death

ers, the Egyptians pushed forward through

PORTSMOUTH, Aug. 26.-At 9 o'clock this
morning, when each vessel Of the French fleet
hove up and Gated one Of the anchors they bad
been lying to and shortened in the remaining
cable. preparatory to getting under way for
Cherbourg, a stiffish gale was still making
matters lively off Spit Head.


While the ironclads were thus making prepa-
rations to leave English waters the French tor
pedo boats attached to the visiting squadron,
which had run into Portsmouth harbor last
night in order to avoid the shaking up which
they would otherwise have received
from the sea running off Spit Head, weighed
anchor and put out to sea, in order to rejoin
their larger and more seaworthy consorts. As
the torpedo boats left the harbor they were
loudly cheered and saluted on all sides.


In the course of time these wasp-like crafts
reached their positions under the lee of the
ironclads, and the entire French squadron
weighed anchor and proceeded westward in
seaman-like style. When the visiting
squadron was passing the British fleet
the blue jackets Of her majesty s
war ships manned the yards, while the
most hearty cheers we're exchanged between
each and every vessel of the two fleets as the
two visitors passed. Finally Admiral Gervais'
flag ship, the Marengo, fired parting salute,
which was promptly answered by the British
men-of-war assembled of Spit Head.

The contest for the seat in the Senate

raiser, who was accidentally killed last
night by his runaway horse. The testi-
mony OF the only eye witness to the

throwing down GARNER, who was then
crushed by the wagon passing over his
head. He expired instantly. The
tragedy took place at 80 yesterday
night.


Leon GARNER was native of the
Hautes Alpes, France, and came here
many years ago. In partnership with
his brother, Camille, he had been sue
cessful for many years in the raising of
merino sheep, and was we'll off at the
time of his death. For several years he

GARNER leaves young wife, but no
children. The verdict of the jury was

Chicago Shippers Demand the Same Rebate


ON Freight Charges Given Others.


Council BLUFFS, Iowa. March PA tran
script consisting of nearly 1000 pages of
closely written matter has been filed in the
federal court here in a case in which the plain
tiffs are j. W. Conn and A. B. Taylor. and the
defendant the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy
Railroad Company.


The suit has been transferred from the courts
of Willis county to the United States court
The plaintiffs. who are heavy stock shippers. sue
for SI0o. 600. which they claim is due them from
the railroad. Conn and Taylor are residents of
Nebraska and have been in the business of
shipping stock for the last fifteen years from
the country surrounding here. the shipments
being made to Chicago. They allege that other
shippers using the same line of railroad have
been allowed rebates amounting TO 80 per cent
from the same points. and that they have never
received any rebate. They now request the
railroad company to refund the difference.
The same question has been passed upon by
the supreme court of Iowa, and it was decided
that the railroad company should allow such
rebates as they had failed to pay.

Erie vestibule passenger train No. 8 jumped
the track at Adrian, four miles east of Canisteo,
N. Y, yesterday, wrecking the engine, the
smoker and baggage car combined, the mail
car, dining car and three Pullman cars. The
smoker was burned and the others badly
smashed up, only two remaining cars Of the
train escaping without injury. The engineer,
James Stickney Of Hornellsville. was killed and
badly mangled, and Firemen Charles Beard
al Of Hornellsville, was badly scalded by es-
Gaping steam, but will doubtless recover. Both
men stuck to the engine to the last. C. Mecrcan
OF Union, mail clerk, was injured badly about
the head, but the other three clerks in the mail
car had a miraculous escape. BaggaRemaster
B. W. Hedley Of New York was injured about
the head and hands, and the news agent ]. W.
Cottreil Of Elmira, was bruised about the legs
and breast, the remainder Of the trainmen get
ting only bad shaking up.


Ihe following passengers were injured: Mrs.
N. E. Bennett, Canaserga about head and limbs;
!. y. Sherman, Chicago, head bruised Elizabeth
Stsidl, New York. dangerously bruised about
head and body; Spencer Bostrick. Owego. NY,
bruised about head; George II. Brown, resi-
dence unknown, head bruised and knee jammed;

ously. excepting possibly Mrs. Steidl, which is

what smashed

An incident which caused much
amusement and set everybody talking
occurred in the court room on recent
afternoon. John Williams, who had
been charged on several indictments for
burglary, felonious entry, larceny, etc.,
but was decided not guilty ON all but
three indictments, pleaded guilty on the
Indictment for larceny. During the day
a rooster was offered in testimony, it
being claimed that the prisoner had
stolen the bird.


Now this rooster, like any other SEN
sible bird, kept its mouth shut and be-
haved very nicely indeed during the
trial. But when Judge Bittenger called
the prisoner up and passed sentence upon
him the rooster could contain himself no
longer, and from within his basket pris-
on there came crow of delight and ex-
ultation. The effect was rather start
ling as well as amusing. The crowd
chuckled with suppressed merriment,
and even the stern judgywas noticed to
relax his countenance little. The mer-
riment at length subsided and the rooster
was voted dandy. But that historic
bird had not yet fully demonstrated his
appreciation of the circumstances to his
own satisfaction.


Williams was afterward called up to
receive sentence on another indictment,
and the unsuspecting people were again
almost electrified by hearing another
hearty crow from the rooster. That bird
was evidently glad that the prisoner was
sentenced and wanted it understood too.
York Pa.) Daily.

ations by the mother and daughter fol.

clusion reached was that the girl had
implicated her brother in order to se-
cure their release from the barge Office.

the dryer path over the railroad ties.

nounced, however. that another meeting

what covering of soil had been
thrown over them, and it looked quite
CHASTITY. Bones wore thickly strewn

miles. From appearances upwards of
5000 or 1000 Indians must have been
buried there.

west side, was found buried clear to the
roof in sand. There are now about 1000

government vessels. and if possible de-
stroy them before they could be reftted

vessels did not expect the attack to be

water and the smokestack of the Lynch

In the meantime the Condell steamed

CINCINNATI, June 3.--0ver 1000 people
went to the Latonia races today and
were soaked through with heavy rain.
Just before the races began hurricane
struck the grand stand, in which were
5000 people-one-third women. The
horse sheds outside the race-course were
picked up and strewn clear across the
railway track, two hundred yards
away. Binding sheets OF water
driven by forty-miles-an-hour hur-
ricane, drenched everybody. The wind
toppled the seats over and rolled them
toward the front; then, amid the
screams ofwomen, avid rush was made
for the broad central stairway that leads
to the plaza in front of the stand. Brave
men rushed into the crazy crowd and
averted a calamity. The crowd went
down safelysto shelter under the stand,
many women tainted. Half an hour
later the crowd was sitting on moist
benches watching the races. No casual
ties are reported.

In Berlin the electric arc lamp poles
are things of beauty. They are more
properly brackets than poles, though.
The taps from the mains in the streets
are carried under the sidewalk to the
house wall and then up to the surface
At the sidewalk begins a handsome
scroll work affair of iron, which runs up
the house and then out over the street,
supporting the arc lamp. Near the base
is panel door provided with lock and
key. Back of the panel is a compart-
ment holding the fuse strips and switch,
and handle which fits on the square
head of windlass shaft projecting from
one side of the compartment.


The lamp trimmer comes along in the
morning, unlocks the panel door, exam
ines the fuse strips, throws the switch,
takes out the little handle, turns the
windlass, lowers, trims and raises the
lamp, restores the handle to the compart-
ment, throws down the switch, locks the
door and goes on to the next lamp. All
this work is done without climbing a
step. The whole device is painted a
dark green, picked out in gilt. Far from
being unsightly, they are real ornaments
to the street. The householders are anx-
ious to have these brackets placed on
their houses, often paying half the cost,
and sometimes the whole cost, for the
privilege. These devices are well made
and expensive, costing about $3.50 each.
Cincinnati Commercial Gazette.

MILWAUKEE, May 16.-The murder Of Aul-
fuss, the old soldier whose body was found
Sunday night in a creek near the Soldiers
Home, has resulted in the discovery that
regular system Of brigandage has -four
ished in the neighborhood of the grounds
All about the grounds and as close to the
grounds as the law will allow them to locate are
low dives and groggeries in which for years the
veterans have been piled with liquor and then
robbed.


The competition grew SO brisk, however, that
enterprising robbers favored the plan Of catch
ing the veterans OH the outside. The grounds
of the National Home are extensive and heay-
lily wooded, and about them are other patches
of heavily timbered land. The grounds
are five miles from the center of the
city and beyond the city limits. SO
that the police protection ia none of the best.
In these woods and along the roadways and
lanes leading into the grounds small bands of
highwaymen, many being composed of old
soldiers who have been discharged from the
home, have made practice Of lying in ambush
for belated veterans returning from the city.


The investigation brought about by the Aul-
fuss murder has developed the facts that
hundreds of men have thus been waylaid
and robbed within the last year. Gov.
Hathaway of the home, has been en-
listed in the crusade with the local
authorities, and they propose to rid the district
OF the robbers. A large force of special officers
are out there and they will promptly arrest
any suspicious parties in the neighborhood.

CHICAGO, July 25.-Capt. Alfred Hedberg of
the fifteenth United States infantry. stationed
at Fort Sheridan, procured a small sail boat
yesterday afternoon and taking with him a
twelve year-old lad who was visiting him and
Private Meyer of his company started GU: on
the lake.


When about half mile from the shore the
boat capsized. The military post was quickly
alarmed with fully a thousand persons, who
could see the three persons clinging to the boat
Soldiers hurriedly dragged out two rubber
boats, the others being away from the post.
These were quickly inflated and launched, but
the waves beat them back to the shore. sud
denly Private Meyer parted from his compan-
ions and started to swim ashore. He rode the
waves bravely. Cheers of the men and women s
cries encouraged him. Desperate but vain eff
forts were made to pull toward him in the
rubber boats. He continued the struggle until
only 200 feet remained between him and tho
shore, when he sank under the waves and was
seen no more. The waves carried Capt He'd
berg, who held the boy on one arm and chung
to the boat with the other, farther and farther
from shore.


When two miles out in the lake the rubber
boat overlook the wreck. With the greatest
difficulty the two were taken aboard, for all
were exhausted. For three hours the powerful
captain had chung by one arm to the boat and
held the ninety-pound boy with the other
Meyers body was not recovered.

A Cape May Point special to the New York
Herald today says: The presidential carriage this
morning was wrecked in the Sea Breeze Hotel
yard, having been out on racket last night
While Mrs. Harrison and her friends were attend
ing the children's carnival last evening William
Turner, the White House coachman, drove over
to the Palace pharmacy to make some pur-
chases for Mrs. Harrison, leaving the spirited
horses unguarded. No sooner had Turner
reached the store than the horses leaped
into the street and started down toward the
beach, where they dashed along the beach
boulevard at a great speed. Nearing the Sea
Breeze Hotel the presidential carriage came
into contact with Adam Lopers wagonette and
smashed it into toothpicks. The presidential
carriage lost wheel but the horses were un-
injured. They were caught after short chase.
Another carriage and pair were hastily pro-
cured. and when Mrs. Harrison and her party
came out from the entertainment she was con-
veyed to her home before she became aware Of
the accident.

SAULT ST. MARIE, Mich, July Ire
ports received here late tonight state that
heavy showers have checked to great
extent the forest fires which have been
raging the past few days in this section.


ST. IGNAcE, Mich, July 11.-One of the
most destructive forest fires which has
ever swept the northern peninsula is rag
ing between Marquette and this city along
the line of the Duluth, South Shore & At
lantic railroad. For 100 miles nothing can
be seen but mass of flames and dense
smoke. Large crowds of men stationed
along the railway track have been fighting
the fire, but the flames are gaining
Roadway. It is feared the tracks
will be destroyed. Between Newberry
and Seny the bridges across the
small creeks are now burning. At several
bridges today trains were compelled to
stop and extinguish the flames. The tele-
graph poles are burned and the wires
rendered useless. Some small villages
along the railroad are in danger of being
wiped out. The inhabitants have been
fighting fire for the past few days, and are
now almost exhausted, and have applied
to the railroad officials for aid.


1t is feared that seven loggers along the
banks of the Tahquamanon and Fox rivers

The following unusually pathetic story is tel
egraphed from Omaha: For a week the entire
male population of Thedford, Thomas county,
has been engaged in a search for the two little
girls of John Hammond, who were lost in the
sand hills surrounding that town last Sunday.
The children, one eight years and the other
four went to visit their sister, who lives about six
miles north of Thedford and between and
3 O'Clock they started home. They had to go
about mile, and the road led through the
sand hills. The children lost their way and
never reached home. The parents and the i'm
mediate neighbors searched the hills all night
and on Monday morning general alarm was
given.


Then the citizens of Thedford and the sur
rounding country turned out. They took the
trail and soon found where the children had
wandered from the path to gather flowers.
The search was continued all day Monday until
dark and the searchers camped on the trail. A
relief party went after provisions and couriers
were kept In communication with the searchers
all day Tuesday as they went on over the dis
NAL stretch of barren land. All day Wednes-
day the search went on.


On Thursday it was again renewed. They
came to place where the youngest had lost
one shoe and could see where the older one
had carried her little sister a short distance.
Thursday at noon the youngest child was found
at the foot of high hill half covered with sand,
where she had fallen completely exhausted.
The little one was unconscious and her tongue
was swollen so that it protruded from her
mouth. She was soon restored. however, and
when asked where her sister was she said Sis
ter went home"

Northern Pacific stock yards, and losing

prodding at lady with his horns at the

Leaving the lady terribly frightened. but

son street 10 West again, where he caught

threw him TO the ground. Luckily the
man was not hurt and the street was soon
cleared of pedestrians, who had dashed

ing Up crates of eggs in front of

Van Houten finally put stop TO his steer

crashing into his brain.

guillotine. Crowds OF the lowest of the

marriage of Executioner Deibler's SON.

prison and execution place. sing
ing, shouting, fighting and using

crowds, making many arrests and some
what clearing the air of the neighbor-
hood. The public resorts in the neigh
hood have throughout the week been
doing booming business as the result

when the police had cleared the streets,
the officers had quite as lively task of
clearing out the most disorderly drink
ing places. Here again many arrests
were made. and drunken men and
women, fighting and blaspheming, were
escorted to the police station, soiling the
very air through which they passed by

profaned it.

text:
WALLA WALLA, July 22.-TSpecial. +
This morning as the Hunt line train was
coming down from Dayton and when near
the farm of Andrew Evans, three miles
east of the city, the engineer saw a man
walking along the track towards the train
The track at the point is perfectly straight
for three-quarters of mile. The man was
first seen by the engineer about
quarter of mile away. When the engine
was about 200 yards from the man the en-
gineer blew the whistle and rang the bell
to warn him, but the man did not seem TO
heed it. Thinking the man would get off
the track, the engineer had not
lessened the speed of the train.
When about twenty-five yards distant,
the man still coming towards the
train, suddenly threw up his hands,
and the engineer, seeing that he was not
going to get ont of the way, reversed his
engine, applied the air brakes and endeav-
ored to stop the train. The engine, how
ever, struck the man, dragged him along
the track about two lengths of the rails,
when the body was thrown alongside the
track. The head was cut in several
places, the left side of the face was all
crushed, and the left leg had been broken
in two places. The conductor of the train
left the body lying there in
charge of q brakeman and brought
the train to this city. Coroner
Y. C. Blalock was notified, and
repaired to the scene. The dead man was
identified as James Studer, who was ex-
amined Monday before the superior court
as to his sanity and released.
On his person was found .
small pocket photograph album containing
pictures of himself and presumably his
relations; also a letter addressed to James
Studer" from a South Bend blacksmith,
and small German Bible. The body was
brought to this city on a hand-car. and the
inquest was held this evening. The jury
rendered verdict in accordance with the
facts


This evening the section foreman found
several papers and letter. belonging to
Studer at a small station called Rulio, on
the Oregon & Washington Territory rail-
road, from which it has been learned that
deceased had been in the blacksmith busi-
ness at Sunset with man named Gully:
also that his mother lived in Bromheld,
Neb. She has been notified of her sons
death

ANOTHER ACCOUNT.


SAN FRANCISCO, July 15.-The Exam
iner this morning printed communica-
ton from its correspondent at Salton,
who made trip by boat from Yuma to
Salton over the Colorado river and the
flooded Colorado desert. Six miles be-
low Hanlon's the party left the Colorado
river and turned northwest into wide
slough, and after proceeding about
twenty-five miles ran into laguna of the
Colorado river. This was the first place
where they saw the water leaving the
Colorado on its way to the desert. 1t
seemed to be breaking out of the river
in many places. There was bar form
ing and the correspondent expresses
the opinion that the river will
probably eventually change it's chan
mel and throw great volume of water
into the desert. There was water all

theirs. For miles from here their course
was through succession of lakes con-
nected by channels from 200 to 400 yards

A number of waterfalls were met with

the sandhills. At some distance after

proper, there entered another stream,
supposed to be Carresco creek. This and
the first-named channel are the only

WASHINGTON, March 2S.-- The weekly
crop bulletin says: The season con-
tinues from one to two weeks late, gen.
orally, throughout the northern states.
Farm work lie generally retarded on ac-
count of cold weather in the spring
wheat regions, and snow and heavy
rains in the winter wheat regions, al
though the general prospects in the
principal grain states are considered
favorable. Excessive rains in the Ohio
valley, Tennessee and Illinois have re-
tarded blowing and planting, but the
growing crops and fruit are reported in
excellent condition. Three counties in
Illinois report that the Hessian fly is
damaging the wheat, but other counties
in the state report fayorably. Indiana
and Kentucky report grain and grass in
fine condition, and in Tennessee much
corn, oats and potatoes have been
planted. Oregon reports the soil very
wet and seeding is progressing slowly.
Winter wheat is excellent. Peaches,
almonds and apricots are in bloom.


CALIFORNIA CROPS.


SACRAMENTO, March 2S.-The follow
ing weekly crop telegram was sent to
Washington, today, by the state agri-
cultural society, acting with Sergeant
Barwick, signal service observer: In
the northern portion of the Sacramento
valley crop prospects were never better,
although the frequent showers have
somewhat retarded blowing and plant
ing. In the San Joaquin valley the crop
outlook is good, but showery weather
would be beneficial. There were light
frosts in the coast counties, but no dam
age was done. In the Sacramento val
ley prospects for large crop were never
better. In the foothills, prospects for q
large yield of fruit are the best in many
years. Grain Is growing well, except
that more rain is needed in the vicinity
of Riverside and San Diego. Peaches,
plums and apricots are in full bloom,
and early vegetables are abundant.


OREGON CONDITIONS.


PORTLAND, Ore, March 2S.-The Ore
gon weather bureau today issued the
following bulletin: The week has been
cloudy, cool and showery. The frost on
the oath did no damage. The ground is
very wet, delaying spring seeding. Win
ter wheat has good stand, and prom
Uses well. Peach, almond and apricot
buds are swelling, or are in bloom.
Fruit prospects were never better. The
backward spring delays fruit and insures
it against possible late frosts. Warm
sunshine is needed. The grass is grow
ing; stock is in good condition.

EDITORS HERALD = Santa Barbara
journals are not the only ones incensed
over the arbitrary acts of the state
board of equalization. This evening the
Express says: "The opinion is general
in this section that the board operates
in the interest of the northern and CEN
trail sections of the state, and this does
not tend to increase with our people the
popularity of existing political arrange
ments."


Other political arrangements would
be separate board of equalization for
Southern California as a separate state.
In other words, the Express believes,
and correctly, that the sentiment for
state division is steadily growing. Some
time ago the same journal, for partisan
reasons, denied this fact; but now adj
mits it under force of circumstances.


The physical differences of the large
area of the present state are too great to
permit political harmony for the neces-
sary legislative needs of the two sections,
and the sooner this important fact is
recognized the better it will be for both
Northern and Southern California.


There was constant clashing OF in
terests in Mexican times between North
ern and Southern California, which has
been continued and increased in Ameri-
can times, and will continue to increase
with the growth of population until any
thing else than state division will be
intolerable.


Already Southern California pays one
fifth of the state taxes, and gets in re-
turn less than none-twentieth. Nearly all
the state institutions are within tide
water CT San Francisco.


Let us have new state in the south,
with proper irrigation laws, represent
alton in the United States senate, and
keep our money at home Git will more
than pay the expenses of state govern
ment), and let Northern California, with
its riparian rights and alleged citrus
belt, run itself.


For THE New STATE.
Los Angeles, August 81, 1891.

The Cinnamon Of Pistsburg, contrary to the
general belief in regard to their burials, do not
send their dead to China, but own q neat lot in
Uniondale cemetery, in which they are in
tered. Yesterday afternoon one of their num-
Der, Jeu Seu. was buried with every rite and
observance attending Chinese obsequies. Jeu
Sen was high Mason, and long procession of
Celestials followed the remains to the grave.
Here disgraceful scene ensued, brought about
by some fifteen hundred Caucasinns, who had
trampled over graves torn down shrubbery
and jostled the timid mourners in order to
crafty their curiosity. The Chinese reverently
placed burning joss sticks, perfumed paper and
printed prayers beside the grave only to have
them almost snatched out of their hands by the
excited mob. They also wrapped small coins
in paper and scattered them on and in the
grave. but boys and men snatched them up and
fought furiously for possession of the curious
mementoes. Cat calls, jeers and howls from
the vulgar crowd added to the shameless scene
that Pittsburg heartily condemns. the excuse
being that the riotous crowd was only made up
Of the idle, vulgar and lawless.

of the island.

tried for burglarizing the Farmers and

lawyers have since been fighting

five in number, being trailed by detect
ives for years, and though fighting des-
perately, legally and otherwise, none
escaping prison save William Burke ,alias
"Billy the Kid, who is believed to have
been killed. Among other robbers were
John Lamey, alias "Molly Matches y

SAN Francisco, May 23.-The Even
ing Bulletin says it is informed through
.unquestionably reliable sources, that
the Congressional party of Chile, other
wise known as the insurgents has en-
tered into an agreement with the United
States government to surrender to the
United States the steamer Itata and her
cargo; that the Charleston will not pur-
sue the Itata any further, but will pro-
coed to Callao, and that the Itata will be
quietly handed over to the American
authorities.


The Pacific Mail steamer Colima,
which arrived today from Panama, re-
ports having left Acapulco May 18th.
Near that port she sighted steamer
flying the Chilean flag, and answer
ing the description of the Itata.
The latter was steering south by east.
Later in the day the Charleston ap-
peared and spoke the Colima. On learn
ing what had bsen seen the Charleston
steamed away to the southwark. The
Charleston at that time was about 130
miles from Acapulco. while the Itata
when sighted was about sixty-five miles
from there. The Colima reports that
the Esmeralda left Acapulco on the
morning of the 18th inst, and went out
to sea, but was seen near that harbor in
the evening. The Itata was expected to
arrive there on the 10Th, and it was sup
posed that the Esmeralda was waiting
for her.


THE EsMERALDA REsoRTING TO TRICKS.


New York, May pa Washington
dispatch says: The coal bunkers of the
Esmeralda will soon be empty. Official
advices received at the state department
show, however, that her officers still
have designs upon the Pacific Mail
steamship coal pile. They are growing
desperate, and are not above trickery to
accomplish their object. Dispatches
from the vice-consul at Acapulco
state that, they came ashore yes
terday morning and represented that
they had just received word from
Iquique, that the Itata matter was set
tied to the satisfaction of all parties
concerned. In the light of this infor
nation they begged that they be al
might Immediately return to Chile.
They did not get coal. Theconsul did
not bite, and he is probably glad he did
not, for he soon learned from Washing
ton that the Itata matter had not been
settled, and that great care must be ex-
ercised to prevent further complications
which might still ensue should the Es-
,meralda succeed in getting coal from an
American company.


AFFAIRS IN CHILE.


NEW York, May 23.-The steamship
Finance from Brazil, brings news OF af-
fairs in Chile. The rebels have formed
a congress with George Month, admiral
of the feet, as president; Senior Eraz-
ariz. minister OF foreign relations; Col.
Arturo Walker, finance; Col. Valley,
minister of war. The first
act passed deoreed that all
articles necessary for consumption
in Chile should be admitted free. The
cities of Valvivia and Tocopiapo have
been captured by the rebels. On April
goth the insurgents ironclads lombard
ed Caldora, killing over 100 citizens.
The next day force landed and occu-
pied the town.


TALTAL NOT RETAKEN.


PARIS, May 23.-The delegates OF the
Chilean congressional party, referring to
the report cabled to Europe from Iquique
that the forces of President Balmaceda
had recaptured Taltal, give different
story of the affair. They declare that
the government warships Imperiale and
Almirante Condell entered the harbor of
Taltal during the absence of the congress
sional feet, landed troops and issued
proclamation in favor of President Bal
maceda; but instead of re-establlshing
the old regime, according to the congress
sional delegates, the inhabitants attacked
the government troops and compelled
them to withdraw. The congressional
delegates also announce that Bolivia has
officially recognized the forces of congress
as belligerents.

AUSTIN, Ga. March 14-Three men lost
their lives in bloody quarrel near Maxey
last evening, and white woman trying to

living near Maxey, was married only a
few months ago. He had among his en-
ployes q negro, named Boyd Hatton,

Hatton met his approach with q dis

revolver and fired, striking Hatton in the

next after that struck Boyd Hatton in the
abdomen. Smith then swooncd from his

to fire second shot when his arm was
held back by the young bride, who was
attracted by the firing. The desperate
negro soon died from his wounds.

sixteen miles northwest, came before the
county attorney at Wyandotte. Kan, last
night and said that on Thursday night s.
s. Barker, 7. Eastman, E. 0verton and J.

vicinity, came to his house, chopped
open the door, seized himself and son,
bound them to fence in their night
clothes and then wrecked the house and
destroyed the furniture. They left Handy
and his eldest son tied to the fence, not
withstanding the night was bitter cold,
and. taking the youngest boy, made him
walk barefooted in the snow half a mile,
when they set him free. The boy returned
home and released his father and brother.

rested. The outrage grew out of litigation
between Handy and Eastman.

OF rising at Vitebsk, the capital of the
government of that name, occasioned by
the peoples protest against the expor-
tation of rye, show q disturbance Of
serious nature. The governor reports
that there is evidence that general re-

grain dealers, who are blamed for the

dered the residences of these grain deal

sent for the assistance of the military,

ers from their positions in and about the
station. The rioters resisted stubbornly
and their supporters outside the rail-
road station made q fierce attack upon
the soldiers, severely injuring many of
them. Finally the officers in command
of the troops, after repeatedly threaten
ing the crowds, gave an order to fire
upon the rioters. The soldiers then
fired volley, killing two peasants and
wounding number of others. The
rioters soon after dispersed. Other and
somewhat similar disturbances are re-
ported from Dunaburg, Vinnitsa, and
other places, but no details have yet
been made public.

PORT LUDLOW, Oct. Especial. THE
bark Sycamore and the schooner Jennie
Stella arrived from San Francisco today.
The Sycamore bore evidence of a rough
passage, and this was verified by Captain
Moore, who reports having met with
strong winds and heavy seas during nearly
all of the twenty-seven days that she was
out on the trip. When ten days out from
San Francisco the Sycamore was struck
with a gale from the southwest, which
shattered her foremast and carried
away her mainsail, maintopsail and
one of her jibs. Captain Moore
very ingeniously iished his foremast with
his mizzen-topmast. which enabled him to
carry a foresail, but he found it difficult at
times to keep out of the trough of the sea,
and was obliged to use oil bags to keep the
sea from breaking over. The Sycamore
will be repaired at Ludlow and load cargo
of lumber and piles for San Francisco.
The Jennie Stella will take cargo of lum-
ber to Ventura, Cal.


The bark Carondolet sailed for San
Francisco yesterday with cargo of lum-
Der and piles.

WASHINGTON, June 12.-Assistant Sec
retary Spalding has decided that queen
bees are entitled to entry free of duty
under the tariff provision for animals
specially imported for breeding pur-
poses, notwithstanding the requirement
that the provision for certificate of
pedigree showing pure breeds can
not possibly be complied with
in their case. This is in har-
mony with the practice under the old
tariff, but is in conflict with the practice
under the present tariff OF assessing duty
on queen bees at the rate of 20 per cent.
ad valorem, under the provision for ami
mails, not otherwise provided for. The
present ruling is based on the represen-
tation that these bees are never inn
ported for other than breeding pur-
poses, and that they are always of su-
perior breed.

SAN FRANCISCO, April 9.-Prospects are
very good for wheat spectators for an ex-
cellent crop throughout California this
year. The comparatively mild winter and
equal distribution of rain have been favor
able for probabilities for good crop, while
the strong European market consequent
upon the failure of the French crop,
has made the Ideal market strong
and firm. Indications for bountiful
season are very good" said Alfred Bannis-
ter. There has been sufficient rain in
both the Sacramento and San joaquin
valleys. and the probabilities are that the
crop will be as heavy as we have had for
some time. Prices are good, and the
market is firm. This market, of course,
follows the European market to great
extent. and that market is strong on
account of the failure of the French crop"


William Dresbach thought that the San
Joaquin valley could easily stand little
more rain, though the Sacramento valley
was in good condition and evidently had
had enough rain to bring the crops out in
good shape. Prices here, he said, would of
course be regulated greatly by the Euro
pean market. which is now strong and
firm. A majority of the wheat dealers on
change expressed themselves as satisfied
with the outlook, and all thought that the
crop would be very good one throughout
the state.

CINCINNATI, Dec. 1S.-A riot was mar
rowly avoided in the county treasurer's
Office this morning. Usually taxes can
be paid December 1st, but owing to an
unavoidable delay today was the first
day they were received. This morning
fully 1000 taxpayers gathered at the
court house, and when the doors were
opened they made rush for the treas
urer's office, all anxious to pay before
Monday next, when penalty of 5 per
cent will accrue. A number of glass
partitions were smashed in the wild
scramble and crush. Five women
and a man tainted and were passed
out over the heads Of the crowd.
The people were wedged in struggling
mass SO that they could scarcely
breathe. Men fought, swore and strug-
gled furiously to get at the receiving
clerks. While the tumult was at its
height the city money was hastily
thrown into the safe and locked up. A
call for the police was sent out, and two
patrol wagons and fourteen men re-
sponded. The county commissioner
finally quieted the crowd by telling
them the rebate time would be extended
to January 10th. The crowd gave
cheer, and business proceeded quietly.
Pickpockets reaped harvest.

pistol in his mouth and blown out his
brains. The affair created the most in
tense excitement in the neighborhood.

SAN Francisco, June 14.--A letter res
ceived at the Chinese consulate yester-
day says the Chinese, All Quong Tia,
having been acquitted OF the charge Of
numbering Poker Tom, Piute Indian,
at Bridgeport, Cal., was dragged from
the courtroom and turned over to the
Indians, by whom he was cut into
pieces. The Chinese consul here will
bring the matter to the attention of the
Washington government.


CHASTITY DETAILS OF THE KILLING.


The Chronicles Hawthorne, New,
special gives ghastly details of the kill
ing OF All Tia. Poker Tom, Piute In
dian, disappeared five weeks ago. His
body was found cut into small pieces.
The body had been packed in brine and
was completely picked. All Tia gave
the Indiar big feast a few days after
Poker Tom disappeared, and served some
choice delicacies which the Indians
greatly relished. The Indians now be-
lieve that Tia made fricasse of Tom
head and heart and served it at the
feast. Last Monday night the China
man gave himself up to the police, as he
feared an attack from the Indians. The
Indians kept guard round the Jail all
night, fearing Tia would get away. Next
morning Tia was arraigned on the
charge of murder. He admitted the
killing, but said it was done
in self-defense. He killed Tom
with club, and then cut
his body up to escape detection. The
justice of the peace acquitted Tia, and
as he was leaving the court room the In
dians bound bim with rope and led
him half mile from town then
brother of Tom cut off one arm. The
Chinaman cried piteously, but the In
dians cut off the other arm. Then they
cut off both legs and his head. They
cut his breast open with a cleaver and
scattered his entrails throughout the sage
brush. Two hundred armed Indians
were present, and the butchery was
witnessed by two white men. As the
sheriff did not protest, no one interfered
with the Indians. The lawyers and the
justice are blamed for acquitting Tia, as
it was known that if they turned him
loose the Indians would kill him.

An excursion train on the c., H. and d. rail.

His Abductors.


DETROIT, March 20.-Joseph Perrien,
the wealthy miller who was kidnapped
in so mysterious manner last night,
returned home about $50 this evening,
safe and sound, but somewhat unnerved
by his experience. He says upon enter
ing the coupe last night, his suspicious
were not aroused until he noticed the
vehicle turned the opposite direction to
his friends house. He then threw open
the door and attempted to jump
out, but was met by two
masked men who held revolvers to
his head and forced him back into the
cab, they following. They then bound,
gagged and blind-folded him, the cab
keeping on, and Perrien was unable to
keep any idea of the locality in his
mind. Finally he was removed to a
room where his captors released him
from his bonds, and covering him with
revolvers, forced him to write the check,
promissory note and letters which were
dictated from typewriter copies
in the hands of his captors,
who remained masked and dis
guised. Perrien was not further
disturbed until late this afternoon, when
his captors informed him that "their
game was up" but that "they would
get him next time" He was then re-
bound, gagged and blindfolded and
conducted from the room. Their course
seemed to lay over ploughed field, af
ter which they entered cab and an
other long, roundabout drive was COM
menced. At last Perrien was unloosed
and thrust from the cab in
dazed condition, and before he
had recovered himself, the cab had
disappeared. He finally located him
self as being at the corner of Myrtle and
Thirteenth streets. He boarded a
Myrtle-street car, and was shortly
home. The valuables he had with him
were not touched. He was furnished
with good food and treated with consid
Grafton during his captivity. His story
is accepted as reliable, and the police
are making every effort to locate the
perpetrators of the outrage.

text:
Cal Mccarthy Gains Victory Over the


Tricky Featherweight.


New ORLEANS, Sept. 22.-The fight to-
dav at the Olympic club between Tom
my Warren and Cal Mccarthy was a
grand success. It was apprehended on
account of the grand Jury indictment
against the principals that the match
would not come OFF, but the state law
allows contests with five.ounce gloves in
regularly chartered organizations. Hence
when the acting mayors clerk received
the opinion of the city attorney that
the city officials could not refuse per-
NIT to the club, there was general re-
joicing by the sporting fraternity.


Mccarthy and Warren were instructed
by the referee that the decision would
be made when it became apparent that
one or the others chances to win had
passed. The men weighed in under the
11S pounds limit. The purse was $500,
of which $1,000 goes to the winner, and
$500 to the loser. John Duffy was
referee. Haley and Robinson seconded
Warren and Omeara and Brown sec
onded Mccarthy.


1t was one of the prettiest and gamest
feather-weight battles ever seen in the
south, Mccarthy winning in the twenty
first round.


In the first round both men dis
played great cleverness from the start.
Mccarthy had the longer reach, and
showed up stronger, and both these
qualities told all through the fight.
Warren displayed his usual skill in
ducking, but Mccarthy found way to
stop his lodging by terrific upper-cuts
with the left. Notwithstanding this.
Warren escaped punishment until
in the frequently recurring clinches,
when he ran counter to McCarthy's
right, which opened gap over his eye.
Thus the fight stood up to the tenth
round, and from that time out McCar-
thy was general enough to keep playing
upon the wounded part. This was easy,
as Warren did most of the rushing and
McCarthy's longer reach enabled him to
counter on the vulnerable part.


Between the tenth and twentieth
rounds Warren rallied great deal. He
stopped number of vicious upper-cuts
with his elbow and found a way to Nc
Carthy's heart and stomach with his left
and swung his right ON his neck. The loss
of blood, however, make him weak, and
his blows scarcely moved Mccarthy, who
kept Warren's wounds open and landed
often enough to sting the little Califor-
nian to madness, and Kept him growing
weaker all the time.


McCarthy's constant battering finally
had the desired effect. Warren lost sci
ence as he lost strength, and rushing
madly struck aimlessly and wore him
self out. He went down frequently in
the twentieth round, and was nearly
knocked out when the gong signaled the
close of that round.


When he came up for the twenty-frst
round the fight was plainly hopeless for
Warren. Mccarthy countered with his
right and left as he rushed in, and War
rem went down on all fours. He tried
hard to struggle up before eight seconds
were called, but fell forward on his
hands and was counted out. Mccarthy
escaped without scratch.


Tommy Warren is not Californian.
He was born in England, and lived in
the state less than year.-SPoRrING
EDIToR.)

this morning Charles Nieman, aged 20,
shot and instantly killed George Me
man, his father. Nieman had been di-
vorced from his wife, but still lived in
the same house with her and their chill
dren. He had frequent quarrels with
his divorced wife and family, and the
tragedy was the elimination of one of
these disputes. He came down stairs
after the boys had risen, and while they
were dressing demanded that the door
be opened, which was done. The old
man then entered the room and began
to abuse his son, and finally assaulted
him. The boys mother interfered, but
was roughly pushed aside by her di-
vorced husband, and fell to the floor in
a swoon. The old man pushed his son
out of the room, and backed him down
stairs. At the foot of the stairs is a
yard. AS soon as he reached the bottom
Charles stepped back, and drawing a
revolver fred, killing his father instant
ly. The boy was arrested, but takes his
arrest very quietly.

WALLA WALLA. Sept 15.-[Speclal. THE prize
hight OF this morning is the sensation of the
hour 1t came off not exactly according to the
programme in this mornings paper, but with
all the brutal accomplishments of the prize ring.
The night was declared a draw at the end of the
nineteenth round, and the stake money was
divided, but Pool was clearly the better man,
and Gallagher was badly punished. His
friends say 1t will be a week or two before he
can be out on the street Gallagher, though
whipped from the start, was game to the last,
and fought several rounds with a broken arm.
HIS wrist was broken in the fouth round.
Gailaghers face was soft and Poole nearly
skinned him. Gallagher's head was terribly
swollen when he reached town, and his face was
black with bruises, while POOLS only injuries
are slight disccoration under one
eye and a few scratches on the hands
To all appearances Gallagher is the stronger
man. He weighs 143 pounds, while Pool tips
the scales at III. Pool is short and well built.
He had been in training all summer and was
in good condition, while Gallagher had been
in training but a short time. Both men are
rallroaders, and came from Seattle here. Gal
iagher has been here month, and Pool came
last spring. Pools friends are jubilant to-
night, and say they will back their champion
against any one of his weight that comes along.


IL was 2 O'Clock Tuesday morning when the
crowd assembled at the cemetery. The place of
rendezvous had been kept secret, but it was
understood the fight would come off in Oregon
The night was dark and cold and the road very
dusty. Two men ON horseback guided the
party. There were about 100 In the crowd on
horseback and in carriages. Sheriff Furnish
and Deputies Haley, Jones and Hickey,
OF Pendleton, were also among the
party, and Sheriff Mcfarland and deputies, of
Walla Walla, were also along. The presence OF
the officers was unexpected, and necessitated
change in the programme. 1t also came very
near producing a battle with guns. Sheriff
Furnish once drew his revolver and leveled il ut
the head of one of the leaders. Many expected
TO see bloodshed, and had a shot been fired the
sheriff and party would hardly have
escaped. The sheriff acted with GOODNESS
and stood much haunting. Both sheriffs
were along to prevent fight in the state but
the officers were outwitted and the fight came
of. Nothing occurred until the party arrived at
Jim McFoots ranch, ten miles from town,
across the Oregon line. Here tickets were
taken at the gate, and Sheriff Furnish forced an
entrance. Day was just breaking. The sheriff
parleyed for about an hour. Furnish told
them he was there to prevent
fight. He was much exasperated by the words
OF the men and drew his gun. Finally the word
was given to return to town. This was blind
to mislead the officers, but more than half the
crowd did not understand, and all were misled
Many returned home, along with the officers
while few went back and staked the ring.


Those who were there said il was the best
fight they had seen. Considerable kicking was
made against the referees decision, and he be-
came angry in the nineteenth round and called
the fight draw. The stake money was only
500 1t is expected that arrests will follow
No one can be found who was at the fight, and
it was given out that Gallagher was hurt by
falling out of wagon.

John B. Smith OF Rutgers College, who is the
New Jersey State entomologist, has been col
lecting information regarding the rosebud"
which is now causing SO much destruction to
vines, fruit. and trees in New Jersey, and the
agricultural college experiment station will
soon issue an important bulletin on the subject


The present invasion Of the ''rose chafer'
dates back six years. and its ravages have been
gradually extending and increasing. The
greatest destruction has been done in the
southern part of the state. and especially
at and in the vicinity of vineland,
where the grapes have been attacked by
the insects and the vines are being almost
killed by them. Fruit trees of all kinds
have suffered in various parts of the
state. Last year cherries and apples were at
tackled and this has been repeated this season,
The Strawberries during their season suffered
and now the blackberry bushes have been at
tackled and first the flowers and then the leaves
have been stripped. The berries, when thew
are well set, are seldom attacked. This year the
bugs have eaten much of the peach foliage and
fruit, and the roses, magnolias, fern and
bracken, and even the oak trees, have been
their food.


Every kind of Ordinary insect poison has
proved useless in killing the insects and putting
an end to their ravages, and even such q deadly
poison as paris green has been unsvailing.
Prof. Smith IL experimenting, and his re-
searches will, he hopes, lead to the discovery of
something that will kill the pests.

The six-year-old Child of Wesley Gorley,

neghbor's, when it was attacked by saw

relaxed. Her tired hands then released
their hold on the dogs throat, when then
brute seized the child again. With no help
in sight, the mother once more choked the
animal until its fangs parted, when she
thrust her arm into his mouth, and though
her arm was lscerated in the effort she sue
ceeded in grasping the dogs tongue, at the
same time pushing the child behind her.
The bravo woman held the struggling brute
thus until assistance arrived, when she
tainted. The boys limbs were frightfully
wounded. while the mothers hands and
arms suffered severely. The child's in
1uries, though dangerous, are not thought to
be fatal. The dog was killed.-St Louis

English policy in the West Indies has always
been an interesting economic study. A world
wide colonial empire had its modest beginning
at St. Kits and Barbados, and the conquest of
Jamaica was the first blow directed against
Spanieh ascendancy in the New World Not
only was the great battle for naval supremacy
fought in West Indian waters but the first i'm
portant colonial industry was established In the
islands. During the seventeenth and eighteenth
centuries sugar was the chief source OF wealth
in Engand's foreign trade. Barbados and
Jamaica had monopoly of the home market and
largely supplied the American colonies with
sugar. The planters of those islands had greater
incomes than the richest English landowners.
West Indian plantation interests for long period
controlled English politics. Burke never felt
strong enough to offer strenuous resistance 70
them. Even Mr. Gladstone leader of Liberal
ism and Free Trade, opened his political career
with defence of slavery and the West Indian
plantation system.


The decline of the prosperity of the British
West Indies is closely connected with the sugar
industry. The first cause was the enlargement
of the area of sugar production. The Lesser
Antillej as they were settled and conquered were
planted to sugar, and with the opening of the
present century Trinidad and British Guiana had
unrivalled resources for increasing the product.
The French developed their own sugar islands
and the Americans opened the Louisiana cane
belt. Cuba and Porto Rico became centres Of
the industry. Nautilus, Ceylon and other Eng
lish possessions in the East enlarged the supply.
The West Indian monopoly was broken down
at a time when emancipation was decreed and
the planters were unprepared to adapt themselves

to compete with slave-owners in Cuba, Brazil
and louisiana they labored under the most
serious Disadvantages. England, by its Flee
Trade system. which accompanied emancipation,
placed the sugars OF all countries on common
level in its own ports. The plantation interests
of the West Indies were Temporarily ruined. A
large proportion of the English settlers aban-
