Little Mary Shaw will live after all, al
though it is acknowledged at Gouyerneur
Hospital that she has had one of the mar
rowest escapes twenty month-old young
ster ever experienced, says the New York
World. All Mary's trouble came from dis
obeying her parents, and her story has a
strong moral for small girls who are too
fond IF having their own way.


The retribution which descended upon
Mary came about in this way:


She was at the breakfast table Monday
with her father and mother and her five
brothers and sisters. The latter ate gladly
what was placed before them and made no
complaint But Mary was critical. She
didn't like the sausage. she had no earthly
use for the potatoes, she scornfully refused
her usual meal of bread and milk. The
menu was not elaborate and her parents
were in despair Did Mary feel sick? No;
Mary felt very we'll indeed. Didn't she want
some of the nice things her brothers and
sisters were enjoying so much? Apparently
she didn't want any Of the nice things. At
this point even the baby lifted its head and
looked at her disapprovingiy. The ShaWs
had never had such time with their we'll
behaved, curly headed little family.


bright thought struck the mother.





the woman filled a large cup and offered it
to her unruly little girl.


Mary took it, For a moment she held it
suspended, while her parents watched her
hopefully, and then, with all the force of
her small body, she dashed it down. There
was shower Of coffee and Splintered china,
q shrek OF dismay from the mother, an elf
ish laugh from the tot who had wrought the
ruin.


Half of the cup lay broken into dozen
fragments. The 0the half was almost III
tact, and lay with the jagged end upward in
small sea Of coffee. Inc little girl leaned
over TO look at her handiwork and, unfor-
tunately for her, leaned too far. The jagged
cup lay in wait The next instant she had
lost her balance and fallen from her chair
with great force upon the sharp edges of the
broken cup.


For time things looked dark for Mary.
From tour-inch gasn in the neck the blood
flowed in streams. There was wild cOnfu-
sion, but no one knew what to do and it
seemed that the child would bleed to death.
The doctor was sent for but could not be
found. The neghbors ran in and the great
tenement was in state of tumult. Finally
the mother found a basin OF water and tried
tn check the flow with wet cloths. 1t was
$3.50 o'clock, fully an hour after the accident
had occurred, when the ambulance arrived
and took the baby away. The blood was
still flowing, and the little one was very
weak.


At the hospital it was discovered that the
jugular vein had been cut through, and that
there were several severe gashes in the
cheek. The ends of the vein was picked up
and tied. the flow of blood was stopped a
bad cut was sewn up, and the physicians at
G0uyerneur Hospital said there was just
chance that the baby would recover.


Yesterday morning this chance had
strengthened into certainty, and when
Mrs. Shaw called at 10 o'clock she was re-
jOiced to learn that Mary was out of danger.
All the prankishneSS and eitiShneSs had dis
appeared and the small girl was very quiet.
Her face and neck were badly swollen ana
covered with bandages. One eye WAS hid
den, but in the other her mother thought
there was a lurking expression which seemed
to say that Mary means to lead a different
life il she ever fluids herself back in her lit
tie home again.


Some OF the spirit which brought on the
catastrophe remained with the victim and
made her one Of tine Quickest and braVtst
little patients the hospital has sheltered for
a long time.

PLYMOUTH, March 1.-THE Hamburg
American line steamer Suevia, concerning
whose whereabouts considerable anxiety
had been felt since she was reported
Thursday disabled off the Lizard, arrived
this morning.


Upon arrival here it was found that the
Suevia's low-pressure cylinders were
mashed to atoms and the piston-rod bent.
She narrowly escaped the fate of the other
vessels which went ashore during the
recent blizzard. As soon as possible after
the accident the Suevia was headed south
ward, with the topsail set. Under this sail
the Suevia continued until yesterday after
noon, when her engineer managed to dis
connect the mashed cylinder and arranged
so as to be able to place her under steam
with one cylinder. The steamship was
then about twenty-five miles south of
Bishops rock. At first she was enabled to
proceed at the rate of six miles per hour,
an d some time later she logged seven and
a half knots, and finally reached Plymouth
without assistance.

Grandmother Connolly, aged ITO years, the
Oldest resident of the Pennsylvania coal
region, was burned to death in her little home
at Beaver Meadow Friday night. She had no
living relatives, and for twenty years past
lived upon the charity Of the people of the
village. Recently she became so weak that she
could not leave her bed, and it was arranged to
remove her to the aims house, where she would
receive good care. The old lady suspected
the arrangement, and, rather than submit, she
set fire to the bed clothing upon which she lay
and was burned to q crisp.

She kept perfectly still because she

strength and skill. When the pack was

row escape With no injuries and only
few anxious minutes she had secured
four dead wolves. worth more than fifty
dollars


She dismounted and slung them over
Pawnees back and then galloped home.


No need of saying that her father and
mother were surprised to see her come
up to the door and exhibit triumphantly
four slain wolvesl


After this glorious exploit the pony
was more petted than before. Did he not
deserve it?-Kate M. Patney in St.

A Demerara correspondent describes a
desperate fight between man and jaguar,
which recently took place on the Demerara
River. The hero of the combat, black
named Lally Davidson. a farmer, was out
with his dog, which reused jagusr from Its
lair. The ferocious animal made tracks for
the thick scrub, followed by Davidson and
his dog Being closely pressed the jaguar
climbed a tree, where Davidson shot it.
wouudng 1t in the head. This made the
animal descend, and again he diyed into the
bush, pursued by Davidson. The beast
concealed himself In some brSmbles. and as
Davidson was again trying to take aim the
jaguar leaped upon him, knocking him
bodily into drain full of water.


Davidson now engaged in desperate
struggle with the fierce brute. and seizing
the jaguar, now somewhat exhausted from
loss OF blood, he eXerted all his strength,
and managed to hold his head under water
until he was slowly suffocated. But before
this the jaguar had severely wounded the
courageous man; his hand was badly bit
ten, the scalp on the left side of his head
was partly ripped off and his left eye was
gouged out. Suffering as he was, Davidson
slowly crawled home, aud while he went
into hospital sent his friends for the dead
jaguar. The latter measured five feet
eleven inches from head to tail. Davidson,
on whose narrow escape his friends warmly
congratulated him. was slowly recovering
when the last mail left Demerara.-N. Y.

BROWNSVILLE, Tex, Dec. 22.-Advices
from Rio Grande City are that troops
from Fort Ringgold under Captain
Burke, Third cavalry, had two skirm-
ishes last night with Garza's bandits
who were seen crossing into Mexico.
Captain Burke had but nineteen men,
cavalry and infantry. Thev were in
formed that Garza's gang would at
tempt to invade Mexico at La
Cruella crossing, and started out
to prevent it. They mounted infantry
behind the cavalrymen and followed the
bandits trail. Approaching their camp
about midnight, they were challenged
by the bandits pickets and fired on
twice, when the United States troops
responded with g volley which scattered
sue them through the dense
chapparal, SO they made their
way to La Cruella crossing,
expecting to meet the bandits again
there. Not seeing anything of them
the troops returned to the scene of the
encounter and ran on the bandits again,
and gave fight, dispersing.and putting
them to flight. The troops had Corporal
Estrome, troop G, Third cavalry killed
and Lieutenant Hayes, Eighteenth in
fantry, elightly wounded. The bandits
were sixty strong and their object was
to sack the town of Camargo, Mexico.
1t is not known how badly Garzas's
forces suffered, but he must have lost
heavily,

A dispatch from Sacramento says that
Geneyieve, the seyen-year-old daughter of
Governor and Mrs. Markham, died at their
residence, Eleventh and ii streets, at 4
o'clock yesterday morning. The child had
been sick for some time, having had
measles, which developed into typhoid
fever. For four weeks the stricken child
had been in a semi unconscious condition
and unable to speak a word. Governor
Markham is, above every thing elSe home
man, and the protracted illness of his child
has not only interfered with his official du-
ties, but constant watching and worry have
seriously affected his own health. Only a
few days ago he departed for the northern
portion Of the State to select resort where
the little sufferer and other members Of the
family might pass their summer vacation.
Friday night, however, GenevieVe had an
attack of heart failure, and her condition
became alarming. kilograms were sent to
the Governor at SiSSon, and Superintendent
Wright made provision for special train,
and the anxious father was soon being
whirlrd toward Sacramento. The child re-
covered from the first attack, and those
about her bedside were imbued with hope
but two hours later a second attack came
and she soon expired. 1t was not until 6
O'Clock yesterday morning that the Governor
arrived in Sacramento owing to an unf0rtu-
nate accident to the train.


The remains will be taken to Pasadena for
burial, near which place the deceased first
saw the light of day. A special car attached
to the Los Angeles train this morning will
bear the Governor and his family upon their
sad journey.

Chicago Inter Ocean staff and the serious injury
of several other passengers, occurred on the
Chicago Il Eastern Illinois railroad, this morn

ing joined his friends on the engine. The acci-

caught and completely buried beneath the
wreck. President Saul, of the c. & E. |. road

wreck as soon as notified. Medical aid accom-
panied the president and everything possible
was done for the injured The engine and bag
gage car were completely destroyed. Two pas
ssnger coaches and the sleeper were more or less
damaged. The roundhouse at the switch was
destroyed and fell upon the wrecked engine.
Fireman Laferty jumped from the engine and
escaped with slight injuries.

CALCUTTA, March 80. Il A dispatch
from Manipur, province of Assam, says
James Quinton, chief commissioner of
Assam, had been investigating some
troubles which occurred among the
native chiefs, with the view of arresting
one of them who was instrumental in
deposing the rajab. The commissioner
occupied camp garrisoned by strong
force of Goorkhas, native infantry in
the British service. Suddenly this camp
was attacked by number of hostile
tribes. A two days battle, during which
desperate fighting took place, followed
the onslaught. The Goorkhas fought
most determinedly against heavy odds,
and, according to the report, 470 of them
were killed. Seven British officers who
accompaniment the commissioner and that
officer cannot be found.


News of the massacre was brought to
Kohima, on the Assam frontier, by two
Goorkhas. 1t originated in feud be-
tween the rajah OF Manipur and lead
ing tribal chief. The rajah was deposed
and appealed to the viceroy. Mr..
Quinton was sent to settle the trouble
and started from headquarters at Shil-
long, escorted by the Forty-second and
Forty-fourth Goorkha light in
fantry. After crossing the frontier
Quinton summoned the chiefs to
durbar at Manipur for the purpose of
arresting the rebellious chiefs. The
tfibesmen, pretending to obey the sum-
mons, mustered in force, and at mid
night on the day before the day on
which the durbar was to be held, sud-
denly attacked the camp of Commits
sioner Quinton, which lay between
Kohima and Manipur. The attempt to
surprise the camp failed, and
the tribesmen were driven back.
They returned, however, and kept
up the attack and siege night and
day for forty-eight hours. Finally the
ammunition of the Goorkhas gave out,
and Commissioner Quinton was obliged
to give orders ''sauve qui peut."


During the fight scouts were sent out
to try to communicate with Shillong,
but never returned to Manipur. The
natives cut the telegraph wires and
killed the messengers. The fugitives
report that general massacre followed
the taking of the camp. There is rea-
son for believing that the estimate that
470 were killed is incorrect


One account OF the affair reports that
Commissioner Quinton and staff were
made prisoners. Another account says
that Colonel Skene, the commander,
Commissioner Quinton, with his son
and daughter, Captain Berleau and six
officers were killed, the natives refusing
to give them quarter. The rebellious
tribe is famous for cunning, cruelty and
bravery.


Immediately upon receiving the news
of the disaster, the viceroy at Simla
summoned council. Two native regi-
ments stationed in Assam have already
been dispatched to Manipur. The Third
Bengal infantry will start for the scene
tomorrow

A special from Tishomingo, Indian terri
tory, says: Deputy Marshal Colcraft has jus,
returned from the Sac and Fox reservation,
where he. with nine other deputies and troop
Of United States cavalry, effected the capture
Of the Dalton boys and their gang for robbing
the Santa Fe train at Wharton, two weeks ago
last Thursday. The trail of the robbers was
found by the Indian scouts and bloodhounds
were put on the track.


The robbers fed to cave in the hills, and
there shot the dogs as they came up, and when
the deputies arrived they opened fire and drove
them back The marshals sent for assistance
and the troops arrived late Thursday evening.
For nineteen hours pitched battle ragged and
resulted in the killing of Bob Dalton and the
wounding of one private.


As the outlaws had neither food nor water
they were obliged at last to surrender and
held ont flag of truce, but as the officers were
afraid OF trickery they compelled the outlaws
to come to the mouth Of the cave with their
hands up over their heads. and with neither
guns nor pistols on their persons.


The four survivors appeared at the opening
In the position designated. but the marshals
were not satisfied with their statement that
Bob was dead and compelled the remaining
members to go back and bring the dead body
IN view This was done, and the outlaws were
bound and taken in charge. In the cave was
found the full evidence of their latest crime,
the robbing Of the train money, jewelry, and
express wrappers were found lying on the floor
OF the place. Two of the outlaws received
severe wounds, and the whole party was nearly
exhausted from want OF food and water.

NEW YORK, Jan. 16.-The baseball war

cesSful season in 1891 are excellent. To-
night the National League, the American
Association and the remnant of the Players
League in joint session formed into two
leagues, absorbing the Players League and
admitting the Western Association to a new
National agreement.


The Boston, Chicago and Philadelphia
clubs of the Players League and the Wash
ington Club were admitted to the American
Association in place of the Rochester, SYRIA
cuse, Toledo and Athletic clubs.

Rochester Club for $780, the Toledo Club
for $500 and the Syracuse Club for $1,000.
The Boston American Association Club
must charge 80 cents admission.


All the Players League sheep must re-
turn to the folds where they were reserved,
but undoubtedly many of them will be
allowed to stay where they are. Everybody
was in the best of humor.


The new national agreement provides for
board of three, which shall control the
workings of the associations. 1t destroys
the sales system and the black list, but con-
tinues the reserve rule in effect. A player
whose salary is not paid may secure his re-
lease from clubs which are in arrears for

rooted from three feet under ground. The
majority Of the business houses are filled with

eruption. The damage will reach $4,000.
The waters reoeded in three hours. but the in
dications are that another flood will come. and
the people are ready 10 fee to the hills at
moments notice.

damage.

Monday William Jones and Chester
Smith, two young Canastota men, came
to Utica to enjoy days pleasure. They
devoted the day to seeing the sights and
expended their money in various ways.
They thereupon decided to pawn two
watches which were in their possession,
and by attempting to do this they fell
into the clutches of the law upon sus-
picion. At the police station they said
their sweethearts, Minnie Perry and
Hattie Daley, of Canastota, had given
them the watches, and Chief of Police
Dagwell used the telephone to find out
whether the story was true. The young
women Immediately swore out warrants
for the arrest of the young men, claim
ing they had simply loaned them the
watches, and United States Marshal j.
E. Stimson came to Utica Tuesday and
took the twain back to their native town.


They were arraigned before Justice
Northrop, and the young women were
not able to establish their charge of lar
ceny. It appeared, however, that while
they had given their hearts freely and
wholly to the young men, they had only
loaned them the watches, but the crime
of larceny was not proven, and the young
men were discharged from custody.


At this point of the proceedings con-
sultation took place Remorse was dis
played on both sides, and some one of
the four proposed that the whole affair
could be nicely arranged in few minutes
by couple of weddings. The parties
most interested agreed to this pleasant
way out of the mess, and Justice North
rop tied the double knot with dispatch.
Miss Daley became the bride of Mr..
Jones and Miss Perry was welded to
Mr.. Smith.-Utica Observer.

train which left here at O'Clock this
morning were 'derailed about two and a

Greek caflon. AS the train dashed

greatly reduced and the other cars were
not damaged. Engineer Morris hand
was severely bruised.

letter was found in his pocket stating that

Asking for the Passengers With His


Dying Breath.


There are heroes and heroes, but the Press
does not know of any better kind of hero
than the railway engineer who stands
sturdily by his engine in the crash of dis
aster in order to save the lives of the passen-
gers on his train. says the New York Press
Engineer Charley Todd of the Chicago
Milwaukee and st. Charles Railroad was
this kind of hero, and his fidelity saved
scores of other people from death, though
it cost him his own life. His fireman
jumped when distractions were sighted on
the track ahead, but Todd remained at his
post With death looking him in the face,
he reversed the engine, applied the air
brakes and opened the sand valves.


This kept the train on the rails, but the
engine was thrown into the river When
they pulled the mangled and dying engineer
out of the wreck his first words were in
quiries If the passengers we're safe. He
expired almost Immediately. But his heroic
sacrifice Of self should not pass without
recognition. The quality of his manhood
honors the race. The heroism he displayed
unshrinkingly was greater and worthier
than that of many a soldier who has died
for his colors on the battle ground, and
whose deeds have been enshrined in song
aud story.

LOUISVILLE, KY, May PA story of
brutal ravishing, murder and swift venge-
ance comes from Eastern Kentucky. Near
Sandy Hook Maud Fleener, a beautiful
young schoolteacher, was met while riding
through the woods by George and John
Wilcox, rejected suitors. They dragged
her from the horse, breaking her legs in
the struggle. They took her to a lonely
cabin, drew lots as to which should have
her, and demanded that she should marry
John, to whose lot she fell. She refused.
They tried to set her broken limbs and
kept her prisoner in the cabin, chained to
to the wall. When found by her brother
and intended husband she told the story
and said she had also been brutality out
ragged. The Wilcoxes were captured and
shot to death by the brother and lover.

PIrTsBURG, Feb. 1.-THE present un.
expected food bids fair to rival that oi
1884. The river has risen all day. and
is still going up tonight. Allegheny
City has suffered most. Several streets
are under water, and at least one thou
sand cellars are flooded. Great appre.
hension is felt there, as two natural gas
explosions tonight have endangered life
and ruined property. 1t is feared others
may follow, as the meters and pipes are
several feet under water and cannot be
reached. The mills along the river have
shut down because of flooded fires, and
thousands Of men are idling about the
river banks.


On the Pittsburg side cellars and
houses on the low grounds are flooded,

out. Any further rise will do great dam
age, as the high-water limit has been
passed. Even now it is reported that
the exposition and other large down
town buildings have been greatly dam
aged,


All the street car lines between Pitts
burg and Allegheny City have stopped
running, owing to the fact that the APP
proaches are several feet under water
Scores OF drays and boats are engaged in
hauling anxious people through the wa
ter to the bridge.


Pennsylvania trains are behind time,
owing to washouts near Conemaugh,
and the Baltimore and Ohio had several
bad landslides. Reports from the head
waters OF the Monongahela and Ale
gbeny rivers, show high water and
general distress.


At Johnstown the dreadful Stony creek
and Conemaugh river stood at the high
est point all day. The heavy stone
bridge caused the water to back up into
town, the greater portion OF which is
from four to six feet under water. Every
house in Cambria city is deserted, and q
swift stream flows through, the streets.


Late tonight the rivers at these points
began to fall rapidly, but the people
will not attempt to return to their
houses until assured that the food is
over. The railroads all about here are
suffering great damage.


Late tonight an explosion OF gas blew
out the entire front of No. 81 Lacock
street, Allegheny. Five persons were
in the house, all of whom were badly
injured. but only one fatally. The
flooding Of the cellar caused the ac-

anti-saloon association began crusade
against open saloons on Sunday. Prose-

cided to close all saloons. AS the state
law also includes every other kind of
business except undertakers, livery sta
bles and hotels, the saloonkeepers de-
termined that if one should close all
should, and served notices accordingly.

house, restaurant, cigar or newsstand
has been opened today. Only one con-
fectionery and two or three fruit stands
in the city dared to keep open, and they
will undoubtedly be prosecuted by the
saloOnkeepers.

text:
It is belief among the German chill
dren that hares lay the Easter eggs, and
the country children go to the woods
shortly before Easter and gather moss,
grass and twigs and form them into
nests, which they mark with their
names, and then skillfully hide these be-
hind the bushes in the garden or under
the large chairs or sofas in the library or
sitting room. On Easter morning they
go and see what the hare has brought.


No one knows exactly why the hare
has been associated with Easter, though
there are many pretty legends giving
reasons, which are as fully believed by
the little German people as the stories
of the good Kris Kringle. The only diff
ference is that one comes at the Christ
mas tide, the other at the Easter festival.
Both are surrounded with mystery, but
both are alike welcome, and are laughed
about and talked about many times be-
fore the happy days come again. Emma
J. Gray in Good Housekeeping.

text:
Details of the Recent Massacre at Takow,


China.


The London Chronicles correspondent at
Tientsin says: "Oficial reports OF the Takow
massacre contain details almost without par
allel, even in the history Of China Previous
dispatches have given but faint idea Of what
happened. The members of the little Belgian
mission had no opportunity Of escaping. The
slaughter commenced with the killing of native
converts, many Of whom were pu. to death
with fiendish cruelty. Children of tender
years were seized by tho savages, hacked with
knives and roasted at huge fire. A worse fate
still befell the nuns, who were subjected to the
grossest indignities, being brutally outraged
by the fends, who afterward Drained them
with massive clubs. The Belgian priests were
cruelty tortured. but met their fates with
Christian resignation. One OF them had his
heart and tongue torn from his body and
burned by the savages in a murderous frenzy.
The most astounding statement is the one that
after the miscreants had been satiated with
outrage and slaughter they were Toasted and
feted by the leading Chinese mandarin in the
district.


The foreign diplomatic body at Pekin are
simply furious. the whole European colony il
boiling with indignation.


The news from Mongolia is increasingly
serious. The rebel forces are reported to be
growing larger and their forward march has
been continued 80 far uninterruptedly The
imperial troops have not yet got into touch
with the rebels"

The fountain on the Clark street side
of the county building was the scene Of
very funny incident the other after
noon. Two dogs, water spaniels, were
trotting north when they came to this
place and stopped for a drink. They
were both thirsty, but neither was tall
enough to reach the trough, and they
talked the matter over as dogs will, and
wondered why they had not been treated
with as much consideration as had the
horses. Presently they solved the prob
lem.


One of them ranged himself under the
edge of the trough, and the other, rest
ing his fore feet upon his companions
back, was able to reach into the pool and
slake his thirst. When he had finished
he hoped down, seemed to say the wa
ter was good, and then in turn ranged
himself under the edge Of the fountain
and the other reached up for the drink
he had earned When he was satisfied
they trotted away together, as well con-
tented as any man could be who had
met problem and vanquished it.-Chi-
cago Herald.

PEORIA, ILL.,, June 18.-A terrible rain
storm swept through the Illinois river
valley last night, doing great damage to
crops, gardens and farms. In Hilton,
across the river from here, number OF
houses were washed from their founda-
tions, and the people fed in their night
clothes to the railroad grade and the
hills. At Farmdale, seven miles east,
the water rose in the houses to the
depth Of three feet. Herds of cattle and
horses and many hogs and chickens
were swept away, and crops for
a large district were badly
ruined. The only fatality reported
was in Copperas creek valley, in Fulton
county. When the flood washed down
the valley, farmer named Gray be-
came alarmed and taking his three boys
aged IL, 8 and 8, he started for the hills.
His wife refused to leave the house, TAX
ing refuge on the roof When. Gray
was half way cross the valley, a floating
log struck and partially stunned him.
The three boys were drowned and Gray
narrowly escaped. His wife was res
cued this afternoon. The damage to
railroads, bridges, etc., will be very
heavy. sv

OTTAWA, H., June 18,-Utica, ILL.,, a
busy little cement and brick manufac-
turing town, was almost devastated by
cloudburst today. Shortly after noon
the clouds broke north Of town over a
high bluff and flood poured through
the valley. The water was six feet deep
in town. Outbuildings were carried
away and residences and business build
ings badly damaged. fortunately there
were no fatalities, but the pecuniary
damage will amount to many thousands
OF dollars.

children were drowned while trying to

village of Hawthorne yesterday, causing
great damage. Crops in all directions
were moved down, and many buildings
badly damaged. The loss is heavy.

William Benson, young man who
lives at No. 432 Temple street, at the
corner of Olive, returned to the city yes
terday, after most remarkable expert
ence in last weeks storm. He, together
with four other men and two little
girls, sisters of one OF the party, started
on Monday in small open sailboat from
San Pedro for San Clemente, where
several OF the outfit were interested in a
land claim. They were overtaken by
the storm, and after being pitched
about for number of hours
of the night, were wrecked off the shore
OF San Clemente.. The frail craft upset,
but the men not only managed to crawl
upon the keel themselves, but also drag
ged the two girls, aged twelve and four
teen respectively, to place of compare
tive safety on the upturned boat. All
OF the party divested themselves of their
clothing and,,s shoes, and thus were driven
by the violent wind toward the island
from point fully five miles from shore.
Eventually, even the support of the in
verted boat was denied them, for they
got into breakers, and rather than be
washed off one by one and lost, they
agreed to abandon the vessel, after max
ing hurried plan for saving the child
rem. The five men were all good
swimmers and finally got all hands
safely ashore some 80 miles from the
place they had intended to reach. Cold
and wet and without food or clothing
the whole party walked for two days
along the beach over the toughest kind
of ground for bare feet, to their original
destination. They were there furnished
with clothing by hospitable people and
returned to the mainland at their first
opportunity, with the intention OF re-
newipg their outfit and making another
attempt anon to assist the colonization
of San Clemente.

Rain Falling In Torrents and the Wind


Blowing Great Guns.


SAN FRANCISCO, Feb. 22.-The furious
rainstorm from the southeast, which set
in on Saturday morning, continued with
unabated severity all OF Saturday night
and Sunday. Rain fell in torrents dur
ing frequent squalls, and the barometer
continued falling. The direction of the
wind in the bay changed from southeast
this morning to south, and increased in
velocity at every moment, until at p.
m. it was blowing seventy miles an
hour. Out on the bay the water
was comparatively smooth, occa-
stoned by the direction of
the wind, but strong tide was flowing,
and this, with the heavy wind, made
navigation difficult. No accidents of
any moment were reported, although
small vessels moored to the docks re-
ceived severe shaking up. A barge on
Mission flats, loaded with lumber, was
capsized by the strong wind and her cargo
was strewn around for some distance.
No one was on board at the time. The
ships at anchor in the bay held their
ground pretty well, although they re-
ceived the full force of the wind and
tide. There were only two arrivals dur
ing the day, the steamer Corona, from
San Diego, and the steamer Acapulco,
from Panama. The ferry boats made all
their trips on time, but there was very
little travel either way. The high wind
played havoc with the lumber piles on
Fast street. Towing was dispensed
with during the day, the various move
ments being postponed until the wind
abated. Departures were limited to
three steamers.

May and June weather with its raw

The Maggie Ross Found Adrift at Sea.


Her Crew Missing.


SAN FRANCISCO, Dec. 11.-News was re-
ceived today OF the wreck of the steamer
Maggie Ross, bound from Coos bay for
San Francisco with lumber. She was
found abandoned at sea and towed into
Yaquina bav. She had about sixteen
hands, all told, but none of them have
been found. The steamer Willamette
Valley towed the steamer into safety,
having found the Ross thirty-two miles
south and ten miles west of Yaquina
bay. The smoke stack was lying on the
deck badly smashed; every boat was
gone, and the steward, H. G. Annensen,
was dead on the deck, evidently
having been killed by the fall
ing smoke stack. The Maggie Ross
left Coos bay Sunday afternoon.
The wind was blowing a gale from the
south, and she must have got the full
force OF the storm. She was driven out
OF her course and forced back to the
northward. What has become OF the
crew can Only be conjectured, as they
should have reached Yaquina before
this. The Maggie Ross was owned by
o. Greenwald of Port Townsend. and
was consigned to the Golden Gate lum-
Der company.


The steamer Arcata is considerably
overdue. She is owned bv the Oregon
Coal and Navigation company.

with terror. Some ran like wild animals,
tramping their slower companions In their
efforts to escape. Others were paralyzed
with fear and stood rooted to the spot with
eyes staring horribly into the roaring fire.


HEROIC DEEDS.


The attendants performed deeds of hero
ism in their endeavor to rescue the helpless,
rushing hither and thither. Dragging hesi-
tating ones from rooms, they drove the in
sane women into the open air. When some
were once upon the outside they would
break and rush for ths building again.
Superinten lent Burr and assistants on the
medical staff gave directions for the removal

cued alive. Nevertheless some say that
several women were seen at the windows
after the patients were supposed to be all
out. They had torn every yestige of cloth
ing from their persons, and were laughing
IN hldeous glee at the approach of the
flames.


PITIABLE SCENES.


BY II 80 o'clock the entire north wing
was wrapped in flames. The attendants
had done all in their power and nothing was
left but to try to save the rest of the asylum
from the flames. Spectators declare that
they heard shrieks of anguish from the
awful pyre as of demented victims yielding
their lives to the flames, but in the confu-
sion it was impossible to distinguish the
screams of the frightened mauiacs without
from the expiring Outcry of the victims
within, If any there were. Strenuous efforts
were made to convey the patients to cottages
for safe-keeping. This was accomplished
with the utmost difficulty. Great fear is felt
lest the fire extends to the south wing,
where nearly 700 men are confined. Prepa-
ratiOns were Immediately made TO remove
the men if it became necessary. Inside the
south wing, from the moment the flames
came in sight, the widest excitement pre-
vailed. Seven hundred crazy men tore
about their rooms, yelling like demons.
Hundreds of people from Pontiac and vi
cinity joined in the fight with the flames.
AT this juncture. and by the most stubborn
resistance, the wing was saved. Aside from
this, everything save the chapel, hospital

At eventide, at eventide,

To tell the beauteous day is done.
The daisy shuts her starry eye,


The tuneful woodbird seeks his nest,

noon. First Mate Murray tells the story of
the wreck. Both he and Captain Cuthell
took observations at noon Monday. They
differed widely. Murray made the vessel
fifty miles off the mouth of the Columbia
River, and Captain Cuthell made the vessels
position ninety miles away, while in reality
they were about thirty. The current,
which here sets strongly toward shore
to the northward, carried the shin
on to the Washington coast. When the
ship struck the officers supposed her twenty
miles off shore. A fearful gale was blowing
and in the darkness the men were washed
into the boiling surf. Captain Cuthel was
the last to leave the ship. He and five
others were drowned. Mate Murray at
tributes the wreck to defective chronom-
eters. Vice-Consul Cherry has decided it is
unnecessary to hold court Of inquiry.

The Chinese raid on WILDLY island was
successful in rounding up ten Cinnamon
who cannot explain satisfactorily their
presence in this country. The arrests
were made Friday and Saturday by Special
Agent Mulkey assisted by Inspector Mum,
stationed on the island, and Deputy Mar
shals Mudgett and Brown. The ten

about on farms leased by Chinese ranch-
ers. All claimed to have been residents a
long time, but could not produce much
evidence sustaining their claim.


The prisoners were taken before United
States Commissioner Cranney at Coupe
vile Saturday, charged with unlawful
presence in the United States. Colonel
Z. III. Winston, United States district at
torney, was present to conduct the prose-
cution.


The commissioner held that the burden
of proof rested on the Cinnamon, and
ordered the entire lot deported to China.
The men were brought to Port Townsend
this evening, and then taken to Tacoma
on the way to McNeil's island. Inspector
Mum has been working on the case for
several weeks. and is well acquainted with
all the necessary facts, knowing all the
legitimate Chinese residents. Cinnamon
in Port Townsend are much exercised
over the matter, claiming that several of
the prisoners are we'll known here, and all
are old residents of the country.

aged eye and iacerated cheek. When

BALTIMORE, Oct. 14.-The train on the
Baltimore and Ohio which left Chicago this
morning at 1910 o'clock met with serious
accident at 2:31 o'clock this afternoon at
Hicksville. twenty miles from Garrett Ind.
The train consisted of the engine, tender,
baggage-car, smoker, ladies coach and the
private car of Vice-Presdent King. The
whole train left the track. and the sleeper,
ladies' coach and private car went over an
embankment. The smoker and baggage
car hung onto the engine and were kept ON
the bed of the road. Two passengers were
killed, and five seriously and several
slightly injured.


The killed are: Thomas Waterstone of
Bridgewater, Ohio, and A. G. Mathers of
Boone, Iowa. Among the seriously injured
are: J. W. Cruback and wife, of Mansfield.
Ohio; Mrs. Sarah Snyder of Porter. Ohio; ;
Mrs. Thomas Waterstone of Bridgewater,
Ohio; Miss Rhoada WOodall of Buffalo,
n. Y.


President King was shaken up. but
otherwise uninjured. 1t was first reported
that the private car of Emmons Blaine was
attached to the train and that he was n pas
senger therein, but the report was learned
to be erroneous. All trains are running to-
night, the track having been cleared.


FORT WAYNE Qnd.), Oct. 14.-The latest
advices tonight from the scene OF the Balti-
more and Ohio wreck assert that many more
passengers were injured than mentioned in
the first report The railroad officials, how
ever, will not talk, and as they control all
telegraph wires IN the vicinity no infOrma-
ton can be had tonight, except through
them.


CINCINNATI, Oct ia Commercial Ga
zette's special from Fort Wayne. Ind, says:
The cause of the Baltimore and Ohio wreck
was the spreading Of rails while the train
was passing through Hicksville at a high
rate of speed. Besides the two killed fifty
other passengers were badly injured, Of
whom ten may die.


All the public buildings have been turned
into hospitals aud surgeons from Defiance
and this place are attending to the injured.
Vice. President King, who was in his private
car, was badly wounded.

SAN Francisco, May 30--The steam

fuller advices of the loss of the British
steamer Holme Edin, Captain Prentice,
which was lost on the Leuconna rocks.
while on the way from Hongkong to
Shanghai. The vessel, which was from
Antwerp with general cargo, left Hong.
kong April 10. On April %, during =
thick fog. she ran broadside on the Leu
Gonna rocks, and in half an hour the entire
after-part Of the vessel was full of water.

nese gunboat Chao Wo. The men suffered

afternoon surprise was sprung on the

start the Bessemer mill tomorrow. To-

Herbert L. Rand, United States consul to
Ponape, Caroline Islands, arrived at San Fran
cisco yesterday. He found letters from his
brother, Rev. Frank Rand. who has been mis-
sionary for sixteen years in the Carolines.


Rev Rand gives the first authentic news of a
bloody war between Spaniards and natives. On
four occasions detachments of Spanish soldiers
effected landing on the islands, but each time
were repulsed by the natives. losing $50 men.
Spanish man-of-war bombarded Ponape, de-
stroying native houses, churches, missionary
buildings schools and the residence of Rev.
Rand, the American missionary, who lost
thousands of dollars worth Of books and per-
sonal property. Women and children were
taken to other islands for safety.


The situation was most critical when Rand s
letters left Ponape. The new consul will APP
peal to the United States government before
leaving this port. asking that an American
man-of-war be stationed mt Ponape until the
troubles are finally settled

What the mammals are in the scale of
creation today the reptiles were in the
mesozoic epoch. They swan the seas,
climbed trees and were most phenomenal
jumpers. Some of them even flew.
While some were herbivorous, living
upon plants, others were carnivorous,
preserving existence by devouring their
vegetable eating cousins. The vegetar-
ian reptiles were enormous beasts, often
as much as seventy feet in length. They
afforded food for the carnivorous rep
tiles, which were smaller than the herb
ivorous kind, just as lions and tigers
nowadays are smaller than oxen.


Though bigger, the vegetarian Great
ures usually had no armor nor weapons
to defend themselves with. Their most
powerful defence was kick, which, de-
livered with hind leg fifteen feet in
length, was assuredly not by any means
to be despised. Professor Cope in Wash

PASADENA, Dec. 12.-The worst storm
that has ever visited Pasadena made its ap-
pearance between 2 and o'clock yesterday
morning. The wind, which blew hard all
day Thursday, developed into fierce gale at
about the hour mentioned, and swept every
thing before it. The storm lasted for three
hours, and it did incalculable damage to
orange orchards and property in the busi-
ness section. The roofs of several of the
largest buildings were torn off and carried
some distance. Scores of windows were
smashed in and the streets cleared of all OBJ
structions, such as signs.


The churches suffered most. The First
Methodist Church was completely wrecked.
The estimated damage is $4,000. The
Christian and North Congregational
churches were razed to the ground. Several
houses in course of construction were blown
off their foundation. Many noble shade
trees were blown down and valuable plants
destroyed. The orange crop was greatly
damaged. At least half the crop is on the
ground, and the fruit on the trees is badly
bruised and unfit for marketing. Many
trees are torn up by the roots.


The telephone and telegraph wires ar
down. 1t was night before communication
was established with Los Angeles. The
Raymond Hotel was damaged somewhat by
falling chimneys. Forty thousand dollars
will probably cover the damage to the prop
erty. The loss to the orchardists cannot be
estimated.


POMONA, Dec. 12.-The severest storm
that ever occurred in this valley began
Thursday, continued all day and till next
morning. There was no damage to build
ingS. few signs and awnings were carried
away in the city. The damage was confined
to shade and ornamental trees and that was
not much. Orange orchards were damaged
some, but few trees were destroyed, GER
tainly not one in five hundred. The loss on
fruit is large. being estimated at quarter
of the crop, caused by whipping oranges off
and bruising many left on trees most heavily
loaded, which accounted for much less loss
than was reported yesterday. A few poorly
built houses were blown down in Lord sburg,
three miles north of Pomona. No damage
was done at Chino to the southeast. The
wind came from the north directly over the
mountains the same as in 1887.

declaring it was q paradise H renegades and
cattle thieves. and no clue could be found.

given him by his son Robert. 10 years old.

nard. Carl Hughes. "Lide" Garfield. Max

gested that they clean out a neighboring camp

Last week, writes "Buckskin" in the
Ontario Observer, in the light of the
moon, two brothers-old prospectors
and hunters, who have been in the hills
for years and have seen many strange
and startling sights report having seen
one of the most thrilling and desperate
fights they have ever witnessed.


They were camping in Gallon that
comes into the main San Antonio canon
from the west, about one and onehalf
miles below the miners camp. The
caiion forks or branches about quarter
OF mile from the San Antonio, their
camp being in the last fork. They had
been out during the day prospecting on
the south slope of Badly, and had start
ed for camp near shutdown, when they
killed a deer, which delayed them till
dark. They hung the deer in a tree
rather than pack it to camp over the
rocks in the dark, the place where they
left the deer being only short distance
from camp, in the west fork of the
cafion.


They had hardly rolled themselves in
their blankets when they heard an un-
earthly roar and scream, quickly fol-
lowed by other roars and screams, as
though a whole menagerie' of wild
beasts had been turned Loose. 1t took
them but a few moments to determine
the cause of the disturbance. So, dress
ing quickly and taking their rifles, they
started to see the fun. By crossing the
cafion in which they were camped they
went over a point from the top of which
they could command a view of quite a
piece of the western caflon.


When they gained the top of the
point they saw just below them, not
100 yards away, what had caused the
noise They could see the tree where
they had hung their deer, and just be-
meath the tree they saS she deer and
two other anlmals-a monster Cali
fornia lion and an immense cinnamon
bear. They had smelled out the deer
and had come for feast, each little eX-
pecting the other; but there they were,
fighting over the carcass to see which
was to be master of the situation.


Their roaring and screaming awoke
thousand echoes in the canton which
made the fight seem more dreadful
still. 1t was a fight to the death. Strug-
Cling and rolling, biting and clawing,
scratching, screaming and rolling did
the monsters fight, only breaking away
from one another long enough seem.
ingly to regain their breath and strength
when at it they would 60 again with
roar and scream. Thus they fought for
over an hour, when, torn. bleeding and
completely exhausted, evidently dying,
they rolled apart, only to lie and snarl
at each other, unable from their terrible
exertions..t do more. But they were
near worse enemies to them than they
were to each other.


Quietly the two brothers, knowing
there was nothing to fear from the two
exhausted champions, leveled their
rifles, and after FIVE shots had been fired
the two mighty brutes had ceased their
struggles, having gained what each had
tried to do for the other, for the two
| fighters of Old Raldy lay dead. Not to
take any chances, the two men waited
until morning, when, creeping up to
their point of observation of the night
before, they saw that the two mighty
gladiators of the hills had not moved
from where they had fallen. There lay
California lion that measured feet 4
inches from tip of nose to tip of tail, q
king of his race. The bear, CHINA
mon, was monster of his species. AS
near as they could estimate, he would
have weighed 1000 pounds. Each was
mass of cuts and wounds. The lion had
one fore leg crushed and mangled. as
though from bite, and the bear was
cut from muzzle to tail by the knife-like
claws of his more active opponent.


So ended one of the hardest-fought
battles and the most thrilling sights
that any man ever saw, and two mighty
mountain rangers whose tracks have
been seen by many who have travelled
over the trails and hills around Badly or
the miners camp, have gone where they
will not cause creeping and crawling
sensation to run up and down timid
campers backs as they lay around their
camn fires ON Old Raldv,s summit

They walked all the way-it is some distance

Pomona Villa proved TO be little house which

One day when was passing the hot
hours in the shaded rooms Of the mu-
scum. surrounded by seated granite fig
ures with their hands on their knees the
coolest companions know, l heard
chattering and laughter. Presently there
came into view ten or twelve Cairo la
dies. Followed by eunuchs and preceded
by guide. The, eunuchs were hideous,
though they represented all ages, from a
tall, lank boy of seventeen to withered
old creature beyond sixty.


The ladies were taking their ease; the
muffiing black silk outer coats, which all
Egyptian women Of the upper class
wear when they leave the house, had
been thrown aside; the white face wells
had been loosened 80 that they dropped
below the chin. Their carriages were
waiting below. The most modest of
men-a missionary, for instance. or
an acknowledgements, suppose, have
put them to flight; but as the tour
list season was over, and as it was
luncheon time for Europeans, no one
appeared but myself, and the ladies'
strayed hither and thither as they chose,
occasionally stopping to hear few
words of the explanations which the
guide "a woman also was vainly trying
to give before each important statue


With one exception, these Cairo danes
were, to say the least, extremely plump;
their bare hands were deeply dimpled
their cheeks round. They all had the
same very white complexion without
rose tints; their features were fairly
good, though rather thick; the eyes in
each case were beautiful-large, dark,
lustrous, with sweeping lashes. Their
figures, under their loose garments
looked like feather pillows. They were
awkward in bearing and gait, but this
might have been owing to the fact that
their small plump feet Gn white OPEN
work cotton stockings) were squeezed
into very tight French slippers with alb.
normally high heels, upon which it must
have been difficult to balance SO many
dimples


The one exception to the rule Of bill
lowy beauty was slender, even mea-
gerly formed girl, who in America would
pass perhaps for seventeen; probably she
was three years younger. Her thin,
dark, restless face. with its beautiful
inquiring eyes, was several times close
beside mine as we both inspected the
golden bracelets and earrings, the neck
laces and fan of Queen Ahhotpu, our
sister of vanity of $500 years ago.
looked more at her than l did at the
jewels, and she returned my gaze; we
might have had conversation. What
would l not have given to be able to talk
with her in her own tongue? After
awhile they all assembled in what is
called the winter garden, an up stairs
apartment, where grass grows over the
floor in formal little plots. Chairs were
brought, and they seated themselves
amid this aerial verdure to partake of
sherbet, which the youngest eunuch
handed about with businesslike air.


While they were still here, much re-
laxed as regards attire and attitude, my
attention was attracted by the rush
through the outer room (where myself
was seated) of the four older eunuchs
They had been idling about; they had
even gone down the stairs, leaving to
the youngest of their number the task
of serving the sherbet; but now they all
appeared again, and the swiftness with
which they crossed the outer room and
dashed into the winter garden created a
breeze. They called to their charges as
they came, and there was a general
smoothing down of draperies. The eu-
nuchs, however, stood upon no cere-
mony; they themselves attired the la
dies in the muff1ing cloaks, and refas-
tened their wells securely, as a nurse
dresses children, and with quite as much
authority. l noticed that the hand
somer faces showed no especial haste to
disappear from view, but there was no
real resistance; there was only good
deal of laughter.


dare say that there was more laugh
ter still (under the veils) when the cause
of all this haste appeared, coming slowly
up the stairs. 1t was a small man of
sixty-fve or seventy, one of my own
countrymen, attired in a linen duster
and travel worn high hat. His silver
head was bent over his guide book, and
he wore blue spectacles. ! don't think
he saw anything but blue antiquities,
safely made of stone.-Constance Feni-
more Woolson in Harpers.

Beckie Brown, the 'sferryman" of

forty years single handed and alone. She
was the widow of James Brown, who

tinued to placidly work at the ferry. In
her early days she attended all the fairs,
horse races and old time musters, ped
ding gingerbread and spruce beer, both
famous, as she made. them herself She

bread that made it famous, and no doubt

For the past twenty years she has

lover of flowers, but her taste rather ran
to colors than what others might call
beauty. She was exceedingly hospita-
BILE, and often entertained friends with a
dinner Of her own cooking, which was a
marvel, and topped off with her famous
gingerbread was a dinner never to be
forgotten.


Her years Of toll and trouble did not
go for naught, as she leaves quite sum
of money to her children. In the fall of
1888 masked men broke into her cabin,
and not finding as much money as they
expected, they tortured the old woman
horribly. The fiends who perpetrated

cred. For the past two years she has

She was eighty-ive years of age, and the

CHICAGO, Nov. 1.-THE stars and stripes
waved aloft tonight after a scene Of excite
ment unequaled since the Haymarket riot.
Over LOCO anarchists and sympathlzers
gathered at West Twelfth street Turner
hall tonight to commemorate the anniver-
sary of the execution of Spies, Parsons ct
al. The speeches were extremely strong,
and red emblems covered everything. The
climax came during the incendiary utter
ances of Henry Weissman. editor qf New
York German trades paper. Inspector of
Police Hubbard, accompanied by Lieuten-
ant Gibbons and other officers in citizens
clothing, approached the stage. Hubbard
ordered the American dag placed among
the flaming red banners which were con-
spicuous everywhere.


Instantly there was a profound sensa-
tion in the motley audience, and the police
were Kissed from all parts of the hall.
Mrs. Lucy Parsons shrieked out: Hang
the murderers OF my husband"


In second pandemonium reigned, hun
dreds of excited men pushing forward,
cursing the officers and seemingly only
wanting word from their leaders to pre-
cipitate a bloody fight. Nevertheless In
spector Hubbard uniiinchingly ordered
suspension of the meeting until his COM
1nands were obeyed. Through the din the
half-hundred police could be seen with
their hands on clubs and revolvers,
preparing for fight which seemed newt
able. 1t was fully ten minutes before
order was restored. The American flag
meanwhile had been reluctantly hoisted to
a place over the stage. This proceeding
was only accomplished when the officers
were found ready for action and the cooler
heads among the audience had time to
exercise some influence.


The meeting had been taken completely
by surprise, else more tragic result
might have followed.


The leaders of the meeting assert that II
was only to show reverence for the men
who perished at the hands of the law.
When the proceedings opened the stage
was fairly buried in red bunting, while
prominently in front were placed busts OF
Spies and Parsons. with characteristic in
scriptions. 1.-THE Marseillaise" was the
favorite music and the band also rendered
"Annie Laurie" which was sung by Par
sons in Jail the last night of his life
on earth. Editor Weissman was the
first speaker and he was fairly
launched in typical harrangue in which
he dwelt on the peaceable nature of the
Haymarket meeting, the prostitution OF
the courts, the poverty-strlcken condition
of the masses, ETC.. when the police made
their entrance and the consequent uproar
ensued. This incident took the life out OF

were very brief.


1t was announced, however, that an
other meeting would be held Thursday
night at the old-tlme headquarters on

The statement having been made and
received with some credence that the
shipments of citrus fruits to the east had
fallen off, that prices had dropped to
very low figure, and that the eastern
market was overstocked with California
fruit, HERALD representative was yes
terday detailed to examine into the
matter, and spent good portion of the
day in visiting various fruit shippers in
town and making inquiries. From these
gentlemen and their agents the follow
ing facts were elected:


At the commencement of the season
the oranges crop promised to be such a
large one that in grading the fruit a
great quantity formerly graded
higher was graded as ''culls." thus leav-
ing the orchardist at this stage with
quantities OF fruit-nearly third of his
crop, IN some instances-on his hands.
Much of this should have been shipped
early in the season, along with the high
grades.


Now, all the high class fruit in sight
having been shipped, the price naturally
falls-not the price of high grade fruit,
which, if obtainable, would still bring
high prices-but of the less valuable
grades, for which less price is always
received. Eastern agents having only
handled the better grades during the
early part of the season, are naturally
not anxious for the poorer quality, and
there is consequently less demand for
the only oranges now on hand; but
prices, considering the quality of the
fruit, have not fallen to any appreciable
extent, and the shipments have really
only fallen off because there is less fruit
to ship.

An English Lieutenant and Four seamen


Risk Their Lives in an Experiment.


Experiments were made in a creek in Ports
mouth harbor, England, the other day with
protected boom invented by the naval commit
tee. The boom consisted OF six wooden baulks,
one foot square and forty feet long, arranged
with the ends toward the enemy. The spaces
between the beams were too narrow to permit
q torpedo vessel to pass through. The obstacle
was solidifed by ten steel hawsers intertwined
among the beams and faulty attached to barges
on either side. To prevent tho impact of o
torpedo boat from dipping the boom and en-
abling it to glide over. another six-inch hawser
was suspended six feot above the boom. The
beams were armed with steel points and pow
erful spikes shaped like bulls horns One of
the swiftest torpedo boats in the British navy,
the one lately commanded by Prince George,
was selected to attempt to pass the boom. The
torpedo boat was encased in a superstructure
rising in the center and sloping toward the ex-
tremltlcs IN order TO carry the elevated hawser
over the hull and prevent the smashing of tho
funnel and torpedo gear. The funnel was con-
structed SO as to fall back if struck.


host Of admiralty officials and naval officers
were present to witness the experiments. The
torpedo boat selected, carrying . lieutenant
and four seamen, whose lives were insured by
the admiralty, dashed forward at the speed of
fourteen knots an hour, striking the boom in
the center. The boat mounted the first fence,
smashing the boom amidships, but the anchor
gear became entangled with the overhead haw-
ser and stopped the boat. Even then the boat
could have discharged torpedoes, but she was
fatally crippled and remained fixed tc the beam.
The bow compartments filled with water, the
boat having impinged upon the iron horns and
the bottom Of the starboard side was ripped
open. The engines being reversed freed the
boat. and it Immediately rolled over on its
| starboard side. The,crew then abandoned her,
and she soon sank.

The Council Will Cut Their Salaries


If He Will Set the Example.


"Look here" said councilman to the
HERALD city hall reporter yesterday,
''your paper is little too previous in
hitting the council. Come here, want
to tell you something"


Then he conducted the reporter aside,
and in dark and mysterious manner
confided secret to the sympathetic
news gatherer.


1t seems that the honorable body of
ward representatives, while the public
has been frowning severely upon them
for reducing everybody's else salaries ex-
cept their own, have really been formu-
lating noble and generous and self
sacrificing deed, which only their regard
for etiquette and the customs of polite
society have prevented them from
carrying out.


They consider that Mayor Hazard is
really the head of the city and that it
would be impolite, inconsiderate, unjust
and several other things for them to take
a step unless he should lead the way.
They therefore propose to follow him by
reducing their own salaries in the exact
proportion that he reduces his own, and
if he in the excess of his generosity
should decide to work without pay, the
honorable council will thereupon
bravely cut themselves off from the pay
roll and serve the city for the fame and
honor attaching to the councilmanic
Office.


The HERALD reporter interviewed
several of the city's law makers who
confirmed the report, but modestly de-
sired their names suppressed.

Just about like you and me.

LONDON, March 13.-The Hamburg
American line steamship Suevia, from
New York February Goth Tor Hamburg,
which was reported yesterday disabled
in the channel, has not yet been found.
Her chief officer, who reached Plymouth
Wednesday night, says the low-pressure
condensing engine valve was found 10
be broken when the Suevia was off the
southerr-most point of Devonshire. A
strong east gale was blowing, and a
heavy sea was running. The Suevia
driited down the channel and expert
enced terrible weather all of Monday
night and Tuesday. Late on
Tuesday her signals of distress
were responded to by q small
London steamer, which, however,
would not attempt to tow the large
steamship to Plymouth or Dartmouth,
for fear OF disaster to the small craft.
Finally the chief officer of the Suevia
put off in lifeboat, and after receiving
a terrific pounding from the sea, met a
pilot boat, which brought him to
Plymouth. A powerful ocean going tug
was sent to search for the Suevia, but
returned last night without finding any
trace of the big liner. Another power
full channel tug was sent out from South
ampton this morning.

Andres Rankel and Angel Montijo
are held at the police station for petit
laweny. The men, who are both Mexi-
cans. are, if the story tol 4 by one Allaho
Buelna is correct, the most ingenious
pair of thieves that have operated in
Les Angeles for some time.


Buelna, who is rancher, came to the
city last Saturday to replenish his ward
robe. Soon after his arrival in the
metropolis he appeared on the streets
with bran new hat and overcoat; a
gold watch chain, at the end OF which
was a valuable ticker, decorated his
waistcoat, and he jingled several 500
gold pieces in his pocket.


The rancher with the Hawaiian prefix
to his name had Lot passed many hours
in Los Angeles, however, before he got
into trouble. He met Rankel on the
the street, and the company being con-
genial, he stayed with his new friend
some time. Rankel invited him to his
house, and the granger, to help pass the
evening, bought bottle of wine.


On Sepulveda street, where Rankel
resided, Angel Montijo joined the COM
pany, and the time passed pleasantly
till late in the evening, when Buelna's
entertainers became tired of temporiz-
ing and demanded all the valuables
which the rancher had about him.


Buelna had not recovered from his
surprise, when he was thrown down,
his hat, coat, watch and money taken,
and his arms and legs securely tied with
ropes.


The conspirators, after this little
pleasantly, hid away the swag, called
the police patrol, accompanied Buelna
in it to the police station, and preferred
a charge OF disturbing the peace against
him, after which they left him locked
up in a cell at the city Jail.


Buelna was tried before Justice Aus
tin, Wednesday, before jury, and con-
victed, but sentence was reserved till
yesterday, the justice being rather
doubtful of the testimony given by
Montiio and Rankel. Buelna told a
straight story, and Officer Vignes yes
terday, after a good deal of trouble,
found another Mexican named Lopez
who had seen part of the affair and
corroborated Buelna's ac-
count of the robbery.


The result is that there is strong
case against Rankel and Montijo for
petit larceny, and pretty good evidence,
also, for forgery. Their arraignment
will take place today.

TACOMA, Nov. 25.-[Special. Two men
were killed and five injured by a landslide
on the Northern Pacific railroad near
Canton, small station between Eagle
Gorge and haywood. In addition two
men who were carried into the river have
not been accounted for.


The dead are:


AsDREw ANDERSON, aged 80: unmarried


CHARLES JOHNSON, aged 20; unmarried.


Those injured are:


JOHN MILLER, back injured.


JOHN AKELUND, lett arm badly broken.


HANS GRAHAM, wrist sprained.


JAMES DoRAN, back sprained.


WILLIAM ENGLISH, confusion of knee ankle
hip and abdomen; probably injured internally


None of the injured are married men.


The missing are:


CHRISTIAN ERICKSON.


J. POWELL.


The dead and wounded were brought
here tonight. The remains were not man
gled, the victims having been pushed into
Green river and drowned before they
could be rescued. 1t is probable that
Anderson was hit on the head with rock
and was unconscious when forced into the
water. Johnson, however, was pinioned
under a huge boulder In the river
bottom, and his companions saw his
hand thrust above the water. mutely
signaling for aid. One daring fellow
rushed into the river, which at that point
rushes rapidly over the rocks, and after a
heroic struggle raised the drowning mans
body up until his nose was about water,
His strength failing, Johnson's comrade
was forced to let the body sink down few
inches, and while he shouted for volun-
teers to aid in the rescue, Johnson ceased
to struggle, dying in his arms. The cloth
ing on the remains was soaked with water


Alter the dead and injured had been
collected, two men were still missing,
Chris Erickson and J. Powell. and it is
thought their bodies were washed down
the river and drowned. Possibly they may
have escaped death and crawled into the
woods or place of shelter. This theory
IS based upon the fact that Erick Larson,
who was flung nearly across the river by the
avalanche of earth and rocks, retained his
senses and swan the few remaining feet
to the opposite shore and then walked
three miles toward Eagle Gorge, where he
was picked up. His ankle is lacerated
and his head bruised and cut in horrible
manner, Notwithstanding which he
laughed at his injuries and joked at his
experience when brought to the hospital
here tonight with his five companions.


When the landslide occurred a gang of
men, nearly all Swedes from the Ellens-
burg division and residing east of Eagle
Gorge, were at work filling In where the
track had been washed out by the freshet
two weeks ago. Above them was bank
about forty-tve feet high. which gave way
and rushed down into the river, tearing
the rails from the ties and twisting
them into various shapes. The gang
of workmen was brushed before the
tumbling earth and rocks like flies, being
literally scattered in all directions EXCEPT
that from which the avalanche came The
track was covered for seyenty-five feet
from five to twelve feet deep. The mud
and water dashed across the river, striking
terror to the hearts of most of the work
men, fully half of whom ran as though pur-
sued by demons. This fact led to the re.
ports that dozen or more had been killed.
At dark several of the men
had failed to report, but 1t Is not feared
that they are dead. Railroad officials are
confident that there are no more bodies at
the bottom of the river where the accident
occurred.


The land slide occurred at $50 a. M, and
the Northern Pacific immediately
dispatched a relief train with the COM
pany's surgeon, Dr. r. f. Smith, aboard. At
Puyallup Dr. Clark, also a company sur
geon, and at Buckley DR.. Sheets Joined the
party. Owing to the washout at Crocker
there was half hours delay, but another
train was provided opposite the washout.
and carried them to Eagle Gorge at q sixty
mile-an-hour rate The dead and injured
had, however. already been placed on the
cars and were brought here at midnight.
The overland train which left this morn
ing was delayed at Crocker till o'clock
and then proceeded to Eagle Gorge, where
it will wait till tomorrow morning in order
TO pass through the district where the
landslide occurred in daylight The
tracks have been cleared and re-
paired. No landslide has ever
occurred at that point before, and the acci-
dent today was wholly unexpected. The
washout at Crocker was caused by the Car
bon river rising seven feet III three hours
ana undermining tracks. The chinook
wind and the warm rains caused the
freshet


Meager reports of terrible landslide and
loss of life at Eagle Gorge have been re-
ceived. Railroad officials are all very
reticent. Little can be learned from them.
but il seems that large force of laborers
were working on the side OF high bluff.
when blast was exploded Unexpectedly.
the result being a heavy landslide, bury
ing a large number of men.

riot OF 1884 here this morning. great mob
of taxpayers ana others crushed into the county
treasurer's Office to pay their taxes and avoid
the penalty. The bills were delayed until
yesterday and it was impossible to take
in all the money presented. One man
put a revolver under the nose of the receiving
clerk and said he would shoot if the money was
not accepted and receipted for at once. The
great crowd on the ontside grew riotous and
hurled stones through the windows. One man
was knocked insensible ana two women were
crushed almost to death. A riot alarm was
sounded and a large body Of police arrived and
by vigorous action cleared the streets and
drove off the more belligerent rioters. There
is great excitement over the affair.

been cut by a white man within five miles
of her ranch. Her household goods were
brought to her from Nooksaek Crossing in

went to work. For six months she saw

She has now several acres cleared, garden

wagon road, chopping down trees,

Omaha Flooded.


OMAHA, June 26.-Reports from all
over the state bring news of additional
damage by rain and wind. Three cy-
clones passed over Palmer, but did little
damage to the town. In the surround.
ing. country, however, crops were de-
molished.


DAMAGE IN OMAHA.


Considerable damage was done in
Omaha by storm that ragged all day
and did not cease until this evening.
East Omaha was badly flooded and the
thickly populated section of the north
ern part of the city was inundated.
From Clark street north toTwenty-fourth
street, the water is from two to six feet
deep in the street, and street traffic is
abandoned. The police and fire depart
ments sent force Of men to the inun-
dated districts to rescue the distressed
people and save their effects. No lives
were lost. There were several narrow
escapes from drowning. Several wash
outs are reported on the branch lines of
the Burlington and Elkhorn roads, caus-
inc the abandonment of trains.


AT NEBRASKA CITY.


NEBRASKA Cry, Neb., June 26.-A
terrific rainstorm prevailed here this
afternoon. Cellars and houses were
flooded. Small grain was beaten down
and badly damaged.

SAN FRANCISCO, June 14.-A letter re-
ceived at the Chinese consulate yesterday
says that Chinaman All Quong Tia, having
been acquitted of the charge of numbering
Potter Tom. a Piute Indian, at Bridgeport,
Cal, was dragged from the courtroom,
turned over to the Indians, by whom he
was cut into pieces.


The Chinese consul here will bring the
matter to the attention of the Washington
City government


The Chronicles Hawthorne, New, special
gives the CHASTITY details of the killing of
Chinese All Tia at Bridgeport, CAL The
matter was reported to the Chinese lega-
ton here. Poker Tom, Piute Indian,
disappeared five weeks ago.. His body was
found cut into small pieces. The body
had been packed in brine and completely
picked


All Tia gave the Indians big feast
few days after Poker Tom disappeared,
and served some choice delicacies. which
the Indians greatly relished. Indians
now believe that Tia made a frIcasse of
Toms head and heart and served it at the
feast. Last Monday night the Chinaman
gave himself up to the police, as he feared
an attack from the Indians, the Indians
keeping guard around the Jail all night,
fearing Tia would get away. Next morn
ing Tia was arraigned on the charge of
murder He admitted the killing, but
said it was done in self-defense.
He killed Tom with a club. and
cut the body up to escape
detection. The justice of the peace acquit-
ted Tia and as he was leaving the court
room the Indians bound him with a rope
and led him half a mile from town. Then
brother of Tom cut off one arm.
The Chinaman cried pitiously but the In
dians cut off the other arm. Then they
cut off both legs and his head. They cut
his breast open with cleaver and scat
tered his entrails through the brush. Two
hundred armed Indians were present
and the butchery was witnessed by two
white men. As the sheriff did not pro-
test, no one interfered with the Indians
The lawyers and justice of the peace are
blamed for acquitting Tia, as it was known
if they turned him loose, the Indians
would kill him.

Receiving Ship Vermont.


New York, March 19.-Just before dawn
this morning the receiving-ship Vermont,
lying off the dock at the Brooklyn navy
yard, was run into by an unknown steam
er, ocean bound. The Vermont at this
writing is full of water, and it is feared
she will sink. The crash tore . hole
twelve feet square in the bow. The col
liding steamer rebounded, and, again
crashing into the Vermont, tore her side
along the water-mark, ripping her
open. There was . lively panic
on board. The sailors were
sent spinning from their hammocks and
the officers from their hunks. Nobody was
injured, but much of the interior furniture
was damaged. The unknown steamer
veered around and made with all possible
speed for the lower bay.


As soon as the marines got their senses
together the first launch at hand was
started out in pursuit, with the sailors
armed for duty. The steamer had the
start for twenty minutes. and up to this
writing nothing has been heard either Of
her or of the launch. When the collision
occurred the steamer was hailed by ths
sailors of the Vermont, but the crew OF the
vessel refused to disclose her name.

BUTTE, Mont. March 19.-rSpecial. l.
The Ella mine, situated at the foot of Idaho
street, was the scene of frightful explo-
sion this morning. by which Walter Tres
trail was fatally injured. Joseph Stuart
ana Kay Crum who were working with
him, were badly shocked by the concns-
sion. The pump was wrecked and three
sets OF timbers were blown out of the
shaft.


When the work was commenced this
morning only Walter Trestrail, Joseph
Stuart and Ray Crum went down, taking
with them eighteen sticks of giant powder
to save climbing the ladder during the day.
This powder was placed near the pump to
tslaw out, and work was commenced in q
level about fifteen feet away. About s
O'Clock Trestrail put in shot, which he
warned his comrades was unusually heavy.
Trestrail and Crum climbed the ladder
about forty-tive feet. while Stuart went
back into the level, where he thought he
would be perfectly safe.


When the shot was fired the powder all
went with it, and frightful explosion fol-
lowed, filing the shaft with flying pieces
OF rock and timbers. blowing the pumps
into fragments and lifting the roof entirely
of. The concussion was so strong where
the two men we're hanging upon the lad
der that Trestrail was torn from it and fell
back to the bottom. Crum fortunately
was able to retain his hold, but it was
only by most violent exertion, the force of
the blast being sufficient to tear his jacket
into ribbons.


Immediately after the explosion powder
fumes began to rise so dense that it was
with difficulty that Crum was able to climb
out. Stuart had been terribly shocked and
almost stunned by the conclusion, but
managed to crawl out through the smoke
and up the ladder. 1t took the men few
minutes to recover and they went back
down the shaft to bring Tncstrail. He was
found stretched across a pile of timbers at
the bottom of the shaft, unconscious from
the combined effects of the fall and smoke.
He had been working in the Ella but two
shifts

The steamship Eureka arrived yesterday
afternoon from San Francisco and sails for
Alaska this morning at s o'clock.


This old vessel has quite an interesting
history. Twenty years ago she was known
as the California, and ran between Port
land and Seattle, making semi-monthly
trips, and occasionally making a trip to
Sitka, Alaska. Captain N. L. Rogers,
present port warden of Seattle harbor, was
captain of her and he says that whenever
her old signal gun was fired on entering
Seattle harbor, everybody in the town
would go down to see her, she being the
only ocean steamer then landing here.


After Captain Rogers left her she was
run ashore in the gulf of Georgia and con-
siderably damaged. Later she was wrecked
in Queen Charlotte sound and her entire
crew was lost. She was raised and re-
paired; she was renamed the Eureka and
has since been run chiefly along the coast
south of San Francisco. She takes the
Al-Ki's place for the present. trip to Alaska,
the machinery of the latter vessel being
out of order.

rioters.

scrambled out as best they could
through the doors and windows, burned
by the stove and live Goals, and cut by
splintered glass, but miraculously no
bones were broken. 1t is said that the

People expect strange and peculiar
actions on the part Of the Salvation
Army, who, with their badges and red
shirts have become as much feature
of life in large cities as policemen and
telegraph boys. So when circulars
printed in red and blue ink are scattered
around announcing meeting with an
odd name or curious performance, peo-
pie only smile and say ''That's just like
the Salvation Army" Such
an odd performance, denominated
The March of the Ten Virgins, was an
nounced for last evening, and HERALD
reporter, who probably needed the serv-
ices OF the Salvation Army as much as
anyone in town, did an unheard-of thing


for reporter-and attended.


The ten virgins, in accordance with the
advertisement, paraded with the army
They were attired in oriental costume
and bore lanterns, of which five were
lighted and five were out, in accordance
with the scriptural narrative. The hall
was pretty we'll filed when the army
arrived at its quarters, and when the
members of the army had taken their
seats the meeting commenced at once.
There was little peculiar aboutthe meet
ing itself. 1t might have been church
prayer meeting but for the real
earnestness displayed. The singing
was good, and though it sounded
odd to hear religious songs set
to the airs of popular street and
theater songs, yet the words had been
written for the music by sklllful bard,
while almost any one could join in
the choruses, through familiarity with
the tunes. Unlike the average church
service, the speaking was all brief, while
the singing and instrumental music was
plentiful and good. Adjutant Boville
gave utterance to a few lively. pointed
words after each speaker, and started a
song appropriate to what had been
said. The audience, composed of very
Heterogeneous elements, kept excellent
order, joined in the singing and seemed
to enjoy it.


Tonight the army has an Indian pro-
cession, or rather, procession of sold
iers attired in the Salvation Army uni
form as it is in India. There are detach-
ments here from San Bernardino and
Pasadena, who will remain for two
days and assist in the coming meetings
and professions.

selves, and this afternoon they went to
their destinations.

SACRAMENTO, Cal, June s.-Shortly after
o'clock this afternoon Silva Perry shot pretty
Mamie Frates and then himself. The awful
deed was committed IN neat cottage on
street between Second and Third. There were
no eyewitnesses TO the shooting. Just after
noon the mother of the girl left her
alone in the cottage while she went to
call on a neighbor Perry was a cousin of the
girl and was anxious to marry her. but the pro-
position was neither acceptable to her nor her
parents. He had been away for some time,
working in a mill on Big river, Mendocino
county. He returned to the city yesterday and
went 10 the house of Mr. Frates, the father OF the
girl, and by virtue of his kinship was accepted
az guest After breakfast this morning he went
away and was not seen about the place again
until he was found lying in the bedroom with q
bullet in his head. He had evidently waited
around watching the place in the hope OF OBJ
tanning decisive interview with the girl From
all appearances he had met the girl at the front
door, but she wished to avoid him and started
to the back room to escape TO the yard.


As she reached the middle door he fired with
3s-caliber bull dog pistol at her, but missed
As she reached the back door. and he was close
upon her, he fired again. The second bullet
struck the girl just above the right ear. She
must have fallen just inside the door that leads
out onto the back porch, for geat pool OF
blood shows that she lay there for some little
time. She evidently recovered from the shock and
swoon that followed the penetration of the bull
let into her head, and endeavored TO escape
The hand rail Of the steps leading from the door
to the yard was red with blood in which her
hands had become smeared as she struggled to
her feet This rail and the steps, some ten in
number, are fearful sight, the first being
covered with blood from her hands and the
steps draggled with that in which her skirts had
dragged as she writhed and struggled on the
floor.

Topeka, Kan, says: A Rock Island
passenger train was stopped last night
near Lymon junction, Colorado, by
grasshoppers. The insects covered the
tracks for five miles, and two engines
were necessary to pull the train through,
their crushed bodies making the rails
slippery. The engines were two hours
in getting the train over the five-mile
stretch. The grasshoppers have only
been Matched two weeks, but it is feared
they will mature enough to rise before
the corn is hard enough to be safe, and
will be blown into this state by north
west winds.

Newton Williamson, who disappeared from
his home in Moran Prairie Wednesday last

air, and box near the mans feet indicated
that after tying the rope to the beam lie had
stood upon the box. adjusted the rope
around his neck and kicked the box from
under his feet. About eight years ago he
once suddenly left home. At that time he
drove to Walla Walla. abandoning his team
and disappearing. His relatives reported
his disappearance to the authorities and the
case was an exceedingly peTplexing one.

gave him up for dead, and were consider
ably surprised after lapse of eight years
